speechtext:
I understand this to be a proposal that in case the company desire to reduce a curve or lessen a gradient all the procedure that is ordinarily applied shall not apply. I can see that there may be good reason for that proposal. But at the same time there may be a very good reason for opposing it. It is not advisable, of course, to hamper railway companies too
much, but it appears to me that the right of the adjoining owners might be very seriously jeopardized by that line of procedure. I do not know whether I am right in assuming that under the ordinary procedure the owner of the adjoining land would be notified. At all events, I presume, if not notified in the ordinary sense, yet there will be registration which will be notice to him, and in this case I presume the whole matter might be carried through without the land owner having any means of raising an objection before the board. I will submit to the hon. minister that this is probably a dangerous change to make in the law. I can understand very well what the bon. minister has in view, which is very commendable in the broad sense, but yet I am inclined to think that it is likely to introduce a greater evil than will be compensated by any advantage that will result from the alteration of the law.

The subject, I am free to admit, occasioned a good deal of consideration before 1 finally came to a conclusion, but I thought it would be as well that this change should be made. I was strengthened in coming to that conclusion by having my attention called to the English Act. It has been for some time otj the statute-book in Great Britain and provides for a possible deviation under these conditions of a hundred yards. One can understand that while you are engaged in the actual construction of a railway thousands of miles away, as in this country, the necessity of having your whole plan recast and of making an application for sanction for a deviaton of a trifling distance, perhaps two or three feet, would be a very serious inconvenience and we could scarcely imagine that there could be any disadvantage which would justify us in refusing to allow such a deviation to be made. The adjoining owner whose lands may be encroached upon or taken for this deviation has precisely the same rights and the same proceedings would be required to be taken as in the expropriation in the first instance, so that, he would not be subjected to any disadvantage at all.
Mr. LANCASTER, I am inclined to think that the hon. gentleman for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) is correct in his objection. The hon. minister does well enough to state that these things may be required to be done for the reasons which he has given when looking at it from the railway point of view, but I have not heard the hon. minister say yet whether the convenience of the public should not be considered a little more in this matter. If the law remains as it is without .this amendment I understand the difference would be that the owners of property where land was going to be taken, by going to the registry office, would ascertain exactly where the lands were that were going to be taken. Let me put a case like this to the hon. minister : Knowing

where the lands were which were going to be taken by the railway by the plan filed and by making a little inquiry about it a man who was undertaking to improve his property would put buildings and other structures in one place that he otherwise would put in another place, probably some 300 yards away from where the railway was to go according to the plans filed. It will be said that if this deviation is made he will be compensated in damages by the arbitrators for the lauds taken and the damage done to his buildings, but no damages in money that a man gets fully compensates him in many cases. The arbitrators have to do their best to see that he does not get too much or too little as far as money can compensate him, but if a man puts his property in shape for permanent living and he has to take the market value in money for damages done to it, such money damages do not compensate it. It is not well that such a state of affairs should be brought about, because, if he has to give up his property, he must necessarily be obliged to take money for the damage done it. The mischief I see is that a man does not know where the railway is going. He has no notice of this deviation. This subsection would take away the necessity of this deviation being registered, as I understand it. I understand it gives the board power to allow any deviation without all these preliminaries being gone through.

I was a member of a delegation from the board of trade, the Harbour Commissioners, the Corn Exchange and the shipping interests, which waited on the government and made very strong representations to the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Sir Louis Davies. A very long discussion then took place, at which the representatives of the underwriters were present. We went over Mr. CLARKE.
the whole ground, and it was decided to proceed as rapidly as possible with the improvements of the St. Lawrence route, both above and below Quebec, and from Montreal to the great lakes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What do you contemplate doing during the coming season ?

I have just read the list of the lights that are under construction in 1903. The fact that these aids were installed during 1902 and are being added to this year has already had the effect of inspiring more confidence in the underwriters. Hon. members know that the Canadian Pacific Railway have been enabled to secure insurance of their fleet at a very considerable reduction on former rates.* It is argued, of course, that the Canadian Pacific administration enjoy so much the confidence of the underwriters that, even if the improvements to navigation were not what they should be, they would receive the reduction. As a matter of fact, it is well established now that these improvements having been made, they have made the St. Lawrence route a great deal safer than it was before.	.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Does the hon. minister know whether the Canadian Pacific Railway are going to have their steamers brought in and out of the St. Lawrence by the same system of pilotage that exists at the present time ?

The law' provides that certain regulations shall be followed, and I think they cannot do otherwise. But the fact is that the six w'recks that took place early in 1902 were fully investigated, and wre have in the department a full report-a very voluminous report-on each and every one, made by Captain Spain, aided by experts. That report is to the effect that not one of these accidents was due to want of aid or improvement in the channel.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: To what were they attributed ?
To fault of the pilots or carelessness of the captains.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

It was my intention to have that document printed and distributed. It is of great importance.

speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I drew the attention of the committee to the fact that the hon. minister's predecessor was so impressed- as I presume-with the importance of obtaining information with regard to the unusual number of disasters last year that he appointed Captain Spain to inquire into the subject and report. I think we cannot intelligently discuss items for the improvement of the navigation of the St. Lawrence, we cannot intelligently vote sums of money to be spent on improvements during the next twelve months, unless we have that report before us. We do not know what the recommendations are, what the causes of danger are, how these accidents might have been avoided or what steps the minister intends to take to avoid such accidents in the future. As the hon. minister has not seen fit to print and distribute that document among the members of the House, we have a right to expect a pretty full digest, in the form of a speech, of the contents of that report. Of course, we do not
expect the hon. gentleman to have these reports all piled up about him, but we do expect that, when he asks votes for such a large expenditure, he will give us full information as to how and where the money is to be expended and what he hopes to accomplish by the expenditure of it. These requests are reasonable and we cannot discuss these matters intelligently without that information.

The information in the department is what I have already stated to the hon. gentleman-that not one of these wrecks that took place last year was due to the faults of the route. That is the effect of Captain Spain's report. I have told him also that I am ready to have this report printed and distributed. But it seems to me that that should be perfectly satisfactory. Now, as regards what has been recommended by the committee of Lloyds there is a large correspondence in the department, beginning in the month of September. There are suggestions made by Captains Wm. Owen, Stewart, Webster, Williams, Murray and Sheldrake for the improvement of the navigation of the St. Lawrence.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Are these the recommendations of Lloyd's agents ?
These are the recommendations made by a certain number of captains who were chosen specially to submit recommendations ; but they coincided entirely with what the agents of Lloyd's recommended.
speakername: The MINISTER OF SIARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Was it the department that asked these captains to make recommendations ?

No, they volunteered, at the request of the shipping interest to make suggestions. The department was very glad to receive these suggestions as a means of assisting in our work for the improvement of the St. Lawrence channel.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Were the recommendations of Lloyd's agents and the captains-
The S1INISTER OF SIARINE AND FISHERIES. They were perfectly in harmony.

Did the officers of the department consult with them on what they recommended ?
The 3IINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. I will read the report:
Lloyd's, September 24, 1902.
To the Honourable James Sutherland,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa, Canada.
Sir,-I am directed by the committee of Lloyd's to inform you that the committee and several underwriters at Lloyd's interested in the trade writh Canada received, with much

pleasure, the visit of the Hon. Sir W. Mulock, Postmaster General of Canada, and the Hon. W. S. Fielding, Canadian Minister of Finance, and heard with great interest the remarks those gentlemen addressed to the meeting which was held here on the 31st July. For your information, I beg to forward herewith a copy of the report of that meeting.
It was clearly pointed out at this meeting that the committee of Lloyd's in their official capacity have no control over the rates of insurance charged by underwriters and that these rates are governed by the ordinary laws of competition. This competition is constant, and effectually prevents any premium permanently rising above the point required for the risks incident to the business.
I am. however, instructed to beg that you will be so good as to inform the government of Canada that the committee of Lloyd's are anxious to do everything in their power to assist them in their efforts to improve the navigation of the St. Lawrence. With this end in view my committee have taken the opinions of a number of steamship owners and others interested in the trade.
The general opinion seems to be that the navigation of the St. Lawrence will always be difficult on account of climatic conditions. The gulf has to be approached along the coast of Newfoundland, where fogs are frequent, ice not uncommon and where the change of variation is very rapid. A ship's position is often very doubtful as the thick weather not only prevents astronomical observations being obtained, but also renders it more difficult to correct compass errors, a matter of the first importance alwavs, but particularly so in waters where there is a rapid change of variation. It is stated that the variation is as much as seven degrees in the short distance from Belle Isle to Anticosti Island.
It has been (suggested :-
1.	That a complete survey of those portions of the gulf and River St. Lawrence (not yet thoroughly surveyed and chartered) should be made.
That is being done.
2.	That the standard of efficiency of the pilots should be of the highest, constantly and rigidly maintained, and that compulsory pilotage might with advantage be extended to a point beyond Anticosti.
This question is under consideration by the department. I hope, before the end of the session, to submit amendments of the Pilotage Act that will satisfy, as much as possible, the shipping interest in this matter.
3.	That the lights in the St. Lawrence, which, with few exceptions, have an average range of fourteen or fifteen miles, should be improved and that the lights and fog horns should have a more distinctive character.
4.	That lightships with good fog signals should be established at turning points on the coast so that a navigator could ascertain his position without going too close to the land in thick weather, such points, for instance, as the east point of Anticosti, Rich Point, west ccast of Newfoundland, the Bird Rocks, Cape Ray and Miquelon Island.
That is being done.
5.	It has also been suggested that better graving dock accommodation should be provided.
The graving dock question is being studied.
Graving docks are not a pressing necessity.

L understand that. I am reading what this committee have recommended.
The committee trust that the suggestions made above may be of assistance to the Canadian government in their endeavours to improve the navigation of the St. Lawrence, success, in which, would doubtless have an Important effect upon the maritime trade of Canada.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your most obedient servant,
(Sgd.) JOHN B. WATSON,
For the Secretary.
The following are the suggestions made hy Captains Wm. Owen, Stewart, Webster, ,T. Williams, Murray and Sheldrake for improving the facilities for navigation of the St. Lawrence :
Rich Point. Should have a fog signal and the light improved.
Flower Ledges. Should have a powerful fog horn.
Heath Point. Interval at present fifteen minutes should not be greater than every two minutes. (Fog signal).
South Point. Fog signal at present a whistle. Should be something more powerful.
Fame Point. Should have a powerful fog signal.
Father Point. Fog signal requires improving.
Cock Point. Should have a gas and bell buoy.
Cape Norman. Fog signal at present not nearly powerful enough.
Bird Rock. Fog signal at present every fifteen minutes, should be less.
Sambro Fog Signal. Should be improved and the interval between bhe sounding of it should be lessened.
Cape Ray. Whistle not nearly powerful enough.
Halifax harbour buoys. Not nearly large erougb, want considerably improving.
Cape Whittee. Should have a light.
St. Peter's Bay. Should have a light and fog horn.
Little Mecattina. Should have a ilight and fog horn.
Matane. Should have fog signal.
Little Metis. Should have a fog signal.
All the captains urge there should be a chart of the Belle Isle straits taking in sixty miles round Belle Isle. At present when in the vicinity of Belle Isle they have to consult three charts all of a different scale.
On the 13th November, 1902, the chief engineer of the department made the following report:
Ottawa, November 13, 1902. To the Honourable James Sutherland,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Sir,-As directed, I beg to submit the following report on suggestions for improvements in aids to navigation in Canadian waters, submitted by Sir Alfred L. Jones, of Elder Dempster & Co., London, England.
In consequence of my almost continuous absence from Ottawa since Sir Alfred Jones'

letter was received, and in consequence of immense pressure of worl? whenever I was here, in connection with the radical improvements we are making in aids to navigation this year, it has been physically impossible for me sooner to give to the letter and its inelosures the attention it deserved. I have now gone carefully through it and examined the charts submitted with the recommendations, and am impressed with the knowledge of the needs of the St. Lawrence route displayed in the correspondence and pleased to know that in very many cases the conclusions reached by the department have anticipated the suggestions ' made by the officials of the Elder Dempster Line.
It is always an advantage for government officers to obtain the views of practical seamen in considering proposed changes in aids to navigation, though seamen cannot always be posted on the practical difficulties in the way of carrying out some of their ideas.
Taking up in order the suggestions made by six of the Elder Dempster captains for improvements in the St. Lawrence, I beg to submit the following notes :
Fog alarm at Rich Point-
The difficulty in maintaining a fog alarm here is that there are reefs lying outside the point, across which, sound will not penetrate. Many years ago a steam fog alarm was established at this station, but the acoustic conditions were found to be so unfavourable that it was removed and utilized at another point. I fear that for this reason the re-establishment of a fog alarm here would be more likely to lead a vessel into danger than to help her.
Fog alarm at Flower Ledge-
This light station is immediately opposite to Greenly Island and Point Amour stations, on the other side of the Strait of Belle Isle, at each of which a fog alarm is already in operation.
The question of providing a fog alarm at this station has been considered many times, but there are quite as many masters, of opinion that, three fog alarms in operation within sound of each other would be more likely to confuse than to help ships, as there are in favour of an additional alarm. The ' Labrador ' side of the strait, on which the existing alarms are maintained, is certainly the more foggy of the two. It is for this reason that the department has not already established a fog alarm on Flower Ledge.
Heath Point-
It would be very difficult, if not dangerous to the operator, to fire an explosive fog signal as often as every two minutes. The interval of fifteen minutes at this station has been reduced to ten and to five minutes whenever a vessel is heard off the station. However, it has for a long time been known that no fog alarm on the Island of Anticosti could be effective, in consequence of the wide extent of shoal water extending off the south shore ; this so disturbs the homogeniety of the air that all our fog alarms on Anticosti have been utter failures, and the fault is one inherent in the locality, which no increase in the power of the alarm would in any way remove. Recognizing this difficulty, the department has decided to establish a lightship in deep water off East Point, altogether outside of the Anticosti shore, and a contract has been let for the construction of a suitable ship, at a cost exceeding $100,000, and we hope that the vessel will
be on h.er station in good time ne>?t season. She will be provided with the strongest modern fog alarm machinery, and will greatly lessen the danger at the dreaded east end of Anticosti.
South Point-
The fog signal here is already a ten-inch whistle of the most powerful type, a signal that gives good satisfaction at many other stations. The fault here is exactly the same as explained above, and is common to all stations on the Island of Anticosti. There is absolutely no remedy for this failure in sound signals due to local atmospheric conditions.
Fame Point-
A fog signal has just been established at this station, and it is proposed to greatly increase the power of the light here.
Father Point-
A seven inch Scotch siren is now being installed at this station, and the power of the light has just been increased at least ten-fold.
Cock Point-
To maintain a gas buoy effectively it is necessary that it should be watched constantly, and that a tender equipped with gas compressors should be able to visit the buoy frequently. A gas buoy liable to be left without this constant supervision would be often out, and thus more dangerous than no gas buoy at all.
In consequence of the remoteness of Cock Point from any headquarters of a gas buoy tender, it would be impossible for us to maintain an efficient service under present conditions. However, the representations made, with regard to this matter will receive further attention, and if anything can be done to improve the present buoy, it will be done next season.
Cock Point should not be a danger to a carefully navigated vessel, as vessels ought to give the shore here a good berth outside of Cock Point.
Cape Norman-
The trouble with the fog signal at this station arises from the fact that there are reefs between the fog signal and the channel, which break up the sound. That the trouble is not with the instrument may be inferred from the fact that the signal is quite as powerful as that at Cape Bauld, only a few miles distant, which has always given great satisfaction.	It is
proposed to differentiate between the Cape Norman signal and that at Cape Bauld.
Bird Rocks-
In consequence of the difficulty of landing supplies on this island, where there is no shelter, and all goods landed must be hoisted out of small boats up a perpendicular cliff, it is practically impossible to establish a steam fog alarm here, and it is very difficult to fire explosive bombs very much oftener than they are now fired, namely, every five minutes, when vessels are heard in the vicinity of the island. The danger here is not great, because the island is steep too on all sides, and no vessel can be in its vicinity without being aware of the fact. It is intended to greatly increase the strength of the light at this station next season, and to render it more distinctive.
Sambro fog signal-
This is another of those unfortunate station* where the trouble is with the acoustics in its vicinity, sound being absolutely unable to pene-

trate the non-homogeneous air that always covers the reefs lying all around the island. When we had a steam whistle at this point it was utterly condemned as inefficient; yet the same machine, when removed to Chebucto Head, where it is now in operation, has proved an eminently satisfactory fog signal. The only safeguard for mariners in fog is to give Sambro a very wide berth. It matters not whether signals are given every fifteen minutes or every fifteen seconds, they would be ineffective, and any vessel relying on hearing fog signals at Sambro Island and shaping a course to hear them, would be more likely to be wrecked than to be guided by them.
Cape Ray-
I am afraid that the trouble with the fog alarm at this station is also the acoustic defects of the locality, but as this has not been proved, and as we are anxious to do everything possible to improve aids to navigation. the most powerful fog signal practicable will be tried here before the effort to make the warning a serviceable one is abandoned. Halifax Harbour-
The whole question of improving the aids to naiigation in Halifax Harbour is now under the consideration of myself and of our local officials in Halifax. Some improvements in the buoys have already been made. Considerable improvements in the lights and any further improvements necessary in the buoys will be carried out.
I may state that these improvements have been carried out at Halifax, and that the gentlemen representing shipping interests of Halifax have passed a resolution complimenting tlie department on what has oe"u done.
My impression is that the buoys used in Halifax are the largest now in service in the Dominion, and that their apparent want of size is due to the great distance at which they are observed rather than to their real smallness. However, this suggestion will have further consideration.
Cape Whittle, St. Peters Bay, Little Mec-catina-
These three points are on the Labrador shore of the Gulf of St. Lawrence, a coast bristling with hidden dangers, and the department has heretofore made a special point of refusing to place aids to navigation on this shore because it is desirable to discourage vessels from attempting to coast it. At none of the places named can a station be established that would not have reefs lying three or four miles outside of it. The consequence is that a vessel trying to make any of these aids would be in danger of wreck on some of these hidden rocks. I am strongly of opinion that it is much safer to force mariners to run from the east end of Anticosti directly to Point Rich or Greenly Island, than to attempt to coast the north shore. This is the more desirable, because fog is more prevalent on the north shore of the gulf than on the Newfoundland shore.
Matane-
A first rate fog siren will be established here next year. The machinery for this alarm is already constructed.
Little Metis-
I very much fear that, in consequence of the Hon. Mr. PREPONTAINE.
long line of reefs exisyng outside the shore at this station, it will be impossible to make the sound of a fog alarm penetrate to the channel. This acoustic difficulty I have reported several times, and feel as well satisfied as a man can be, without actually experimenting, that a fog alarm here would be a failure, and therefore a snare to a sailor rather than a help.
The chart of the Strait of Belle Isle is a matter in the hands of the Hydrographer of the Admiralty, and not of the Canadian government. I have no doubt that representations from the shipping interests of Great Britain . made to the Lords of the Admiralty would result in the production of a chart such as desired by the Elder Dempster Company's captains. I know that what they s*ate with regard to this matter is perfectly true, and I suggest that this department join in representing to the Admiralty the desirability of having a large scale chart of the approach of Belle Isle from the outside.
As the Admiralty is now engaged in a resurvey of Newfoundland, I am sure they would the more readily grant such a request.

Whose report is that ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. It is the report of the chief engineer, Mr. Anderson.

Sent in reply to the letter with some inclosures of Sir Alfred Jones ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Yes.

Is not Sir Alfred Jones' letter there ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. I have not the letter of Sir Alfred Jones, but as I remarked, the engineer goes over every point that has been suggested by Sir Alfred Jones and the captains who were delegated to make suggestions.
The	MINISTER	OF	JUSTICE	(Hon.
Charles Fitzpatrick.) I would like if the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries could tell me where the ' Sahara ' was wrecked, at what season of the year she was wrecked, and whether or not there was a pilot on board ?	*
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. She had no pilot on board, and she simply went out of her course.

I can scarcely understand why it is that so much complaint is made about the condition of the St. Lawrence route when my hon. friend bears in mind that this ship came up with a valuable cargo of rice in April or May, and instead of staying at pilotage ground, as she ought to have done, proceeded without a pilot. When she reached Sydney, the captain notified the agent in Quebec that the vessel was coming up and asked him to have a pilot ready, but instead of waiting at the pilotage ground the vessel came on up towards Rimouski and ran right on a rock. My information is to the effect that

the captain had never been on the St. Lawrence before. He came up in the early spring and did not take the trouble to get a pilot on board and the vessel ran on the rocks. There is another case of a ship, the name of which I do not recollect at this moment, that ran on the west point of Anti-c-osti Island, a ship that was going down the St. Lawrence and supposed to be going to [DOT]sea, but the first thing we heard that the ship was aground on the west point of Anticosti. Investigations were held into the cause of these accidents, and I think it would be important not only for the information of the House, but for the information of the public, and especially for the information of the underwriters in London, that the results of these inquiries should be published so as to show whether or not these accidents have been caused exclusively by the conditions existing on the St. Lawrence route, or by defective equipment of the ships, or whether they have been caused by any defect or neglect on the part of the captains. I remember that last summer I attended an inquiry at Quebec. where it was shown that the captain, while going through the Traverse, one of the most dangerous points on the St. Lawrence. thought it proper to go down and go to bed and leave bis ship under the control of the pilot and one of the subordinate officers. If, under these circumstances, accidents happen the underwriters must not be surprised, and it seems to me that it would be important to know all the facts and circumstances connected with each one of these wrecks so that we may know whether the fault is attributable to any defect in the condition of the St. Lawrence route or to the unskilful mariner who is in charge of the vessel, or to the fact of negligence on the part of the mariner. I think it will be shown in most cases that the accident is more the result of the imperfect equipment of the ship, or of negligence on the part of the captain, than as a result of the conditions of the St. Lawrence route. Let me illustrate what I mean. Last summer the ' Ariadne,' Admiral Douglas' vessel, came up from Halifax to Quebec. The sailing captain started from Halifax and brought his ship to Quebec on his own chart-a vessel drawing thirty feet of water-without the slightest difficulty.
Is it not a fact that admirals in the imperial service are obliged to do that ?

In the imperial service they have proper officers and properly equipped vessels, and when they came to the St. Lawrence they navigated the river without difficulty. The only accident that happened on the St. Lawrence route to an imperial vessel was in the case of a ship going from Quebec to Montreal and the accident happened when there was a pilot in charge. She had just left the harbour of Quebec when she ran aground.
I agree with all that the hon. gentleman said in respect to the improvement of the aids to navigation in the lower St. Lawrence. It is important to do all that we can do to improve the condition of the St. Lawrence route, so that that great waterway may be from the great lakes to the ocean as perfectly equipped as any great waterway can be. Nature has given us the greatest waterway on the continent and it only remains for us to so equip and improve that waterway that we may be able to avail ourselves of the great advantages that may come to it. We must not only spend our money in the way of dredging, but it is also important that we shall provide those aids to navigation which will enable the mariners to take advantage of the work we are doing. I venture to make the suggestion that we ought to take advantage of the information afforded by the officers in our department. These officers are competent men and we should also at the same time, if necessary-and I offer this suggestion because of the interest I have in that part of the country-consult the Lloyds people and say that we would be willing to pay the expenses of any competent man they would suggest to come out and visit the work we are doing and make such suggestions as they thought necessary in order that we might meet all reasonable demands of the underwriters. I would also suggest that when an accident occurs we should thoroughly probe the cause of the accident, so that we may know whether or not it was caused through any defect in the St. Lawrence route, or whether through the defective equipment of the vessel or defective seamanship. It is important in cases of accidents to know exactly what has been the cause of the accident, and I think that when we hare done that we will show that the St. Lawrence has been very much maligned in the past and that a great many accidents that have occurred have not been due to any defect in the St. Lawrence route, but that they have been due to defects in the equipment of vessels and to the imperfect knowledge of the seamen passing through that route.

I may say that the hon. Minister of Justice is to be congratulated upon coming to our assistance on this side of the House in demanding that the information which we have been trying to obtain from the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries shall be forthcoming as soon as possible.
There is no politics in this question.

Certainly not, and we could not have approached it on this side of the House with any desire to make political capital, because, in the few remarks I have made, I declared that we were quite willing to vote any reasonable sum to equip that route and to make it the best route on

this side of the Atlantic. I think the kon. minister can appreciate the difficulties which landlubbers like myself labour under iu intelligently voting the appropriation that is now asked for by the department when the fullest possible information is not vouchsafed to us as to what these expenditures are for and why they are being asked for. The hon. minister has drawn attention to the fact that the injury which happened the steamship ' Sahara ' was duo to the circumstance that she had not a pilot on board and that the captain was practically in ignorance of the route.

This report will be printed and distributed. I am able to state from the information of the officers of the department that a separate document will be printed and distributed because the report of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries contains Captain Spain's report, dated 23rd of September.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I must confess that I was not aware of that fact and I am very glad to know it. I have read from two editions of the London ' Times ' unfavourable references to the St. Lawrence route. I did so for the purpose of drawing the attention ot the committee and of the hon. minister to the fact that the route is being misrepresented and that unreasonable insurance charges are being made upon vessels navigating it. It is of the highest importance, as the Minister of Justice has pointed out, that when an accident occurs the causes should be inquired into forthwith and the blame placed on the responsible shoulders. If wide pub-lidty were given to the findings of the commissioners. the black eyes that the St. Lawrence route receives from time to time would be less frequent. Our desire is not to make political capital, but to have at our disposal all the data jn possession of the department' so that we may vote these items intelligently. Can we have that lettei from Sir Alfred Jones.
Certainly,, it will be laid on the Table.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I draw attention to the fact that although navigation has only been opened a few weeks, whatever may be the cause, there have been two accidents, and not to large ships but to moderate sized vessels. I hope the minister will have an immediate investigation into both. It is sometimes said that the pilotage system is defective.
Very.
The Minister of Justice holds that sometimes those in charge of the navigation of the ship are to blame, and that state of things can certainly be remedied.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) will look at the Mr. CLARKE.
plans that have been prepared within the last year or two in reference to the lower St. Lawrence, he will see that a comprehensive scheme is ready for endeavouring to supply those aids to navigation which are so necessary. Last year over $200,000 was expended in the carrying out of this scheme, and if we proceed on these lines in the future we will soon equip the St. Lawrence as it ought to have been equipped years ago. But that is not all. The pilots are an essential factor in the navigation of the St. Lawrence and it seems to me that the sooner we take effective control over the pilots the better it is going to be. It would be absolutely useless for us to expend our money on aids to navigation if we have a defective pilotage system.
Some hou. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

The sooner that is realized the better for all concerned. I make the statement, subject to correction, that the pilots are not examined with respect to coloured blindness except only once a year. There is nothing more important than that the vision of the pilot should be perfect; not only that it should be perfect with respect to distance, but also with respect to colour so much depends upon the colour of the light, not only the port and starboard lights of the ship, but the lights on the shore. It is well known that railway locomotive engineers are examined every two or three months to test their sight as to colour. It is as essential, if not more essential, that the vision of the pilot should be perfect than the vision of the railway engineer. If my hon. friend looks at the rules that exist on the Mersey he will notice the great caution that is exercised there with respect to the pilotage system. On the St. Lawrence where we have equal opportunities to afford a safe way for navigation as they have on the Mersey and the English channel generally, it seems to me we ought be able to do for the St. Lawrence what the English authorities have been able to do for the navigation of the English channel and the Mersey. I trust that we may be able to follow their example as closely as we can.
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) refers to the report of the Marine Department, 1902, pages 27 to 40, he will find the reports on the accidents that have occurred in the St. Lawrence.

speechtext: Before leaving this part of the discussion I wish to express my regret that the department did not print in its annual report the results of the investigations held in Great Britain in connection with the accidents on the St. Lawrence. In almost every case where an investigation was held by the British Board of Trade it was found that the accidents were due to negligence or want of knowledge on the part of the steamships' officers. That is a thing that should be known not only on this side of the water, but on the other side as Well. If the Minister of Marine and Fisheries printed these investigations in his report it would have the effect of removing to a great extent the misrepresentations with regard to the St. Lawrence route. As I say, these English investigations show that in almost every case for the past two years, the accident was the result of incompetency or neglect on the part of the steamships' officers. I do not say that at all to imply that the aids to navigation should not be continued in the direction we have commenced, or that in every case where the system is found to be defective, a better system should not be adopted. At the same time it should be known here and throughout the world that the route is not at all to be blamed to anything like the extent which it is understood to be, both in this country and the old country.

speechtext: I would like to draw the attention of the hon. member for Toronto to the report of the inquiry into eleven casualties in the St. Lawrence river. He will find that the result of this investigation is that five casualties were caused by the inexperience or carelessness of some one or more of the officers or pilots on board the ships, but in not one case was the accident caused by inefficiency or deficiency in the aids to navigation.
Do I understand the ex-Miuister of Marine and Fisheries regrets that the English report has not been published or circulated ?

I think the department intended to have published the results of the investigation in Great Britain, which was furnished to us in a return from the Board of Trade, under whose auspices these investigations are held. I think it would be a good investment and a proper thing for the House to order that that report should be printed as a return and distributed both here and in Great Britain.

We have the findings of Mr. Spain, the commissioner, but we have not the evidence before us. In the report there is a very remarkable statement made, which I cannot altogether fathom. It is as follows :

He is going to be proceeded against. We discovered that from the report handed to the department a few days ago. Another vessel 'The Carrigan Head,' went ashore near the same point. The result was that the light-keeper was dismissed, and replaced by a competent man. It is proposed by the department, in order to avoid any such accidents in future, to have a small boat to patrol the channel, especially between Quebec and Montreal, as is done between Montreal and Kingston, to ascertain every twenty-four or forty-eight hours the state of the buoys, and to see that they have not been dragged or displaced. That has been suggested to the department, as a result of these two last accidents, so that the department is perfectly alive to the situation. With regard to the aids to navigation, we know the sentiment of the House. There is no politics in this matter. Everybody agrees that, in the interest of trade and commerce and of navigation, the route of the St. Lawrence should be made perfectly safe. I may state that it is the intention of the department this season to have the channel between Montreal and Sorel, a length of forty-five miles, perfectly lighted, so that in that stretch the navigation of the river will be as safe during night as during day. It will probably be impossible for two or three years to have all the necessary aids to navigation between Sorel and Quebec, on account of the channel at certain points especially at Cap a La Roche, not having the proper width; and not offering security to steamers to navigate that channel during the night. But between Sorel and Montreal, by the 1st of July, or at the latest by the 1st of August, the channel will be perfectly lighted on both sides.

speechtext: I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that there should be no politics in this matter at all; and, so far as I am concerned, there is no politics. It is a very serious question, and one that has been discussed for years, and I do not think we should do anything to discourage trade from going over the St. Lawrence route. When a statement of this character is made, I would like to know, whether the owners of the vessels are ever present at these investigations ^nd in what manner they show their indifference ?

I have pointed out the fact that the owners were informed that the vessels had touched at that point, but rather than bo troubled by an investigation or detained, they preferred not to mention it, and the vessel went back without any investigation being held.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: With respect to the indifference of the owners, my hon. friend will bear in mind that the great majority of the owners reside on the other side of the water and also that a great number of the steamers are owned by many people. A ship is divided into sixty-four shares, and in many cases there are as many as sixty-four owners to one ship. The agent at Quebec or at Montreal represents the owners. When an accident occurs, in nine cases out of ten, the vessel is abandoned to the underwriters and the owners pay no more attention to the matter. They simply wash their hands of the whole affair and leave it on the shoulders of the unfortunate underwriters. Last year I am informed, and my information can be verified by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock), that a vessel of the value of $500,000 came to the St. Lawrence aud was penalized to this extent, that the owner paid for insurance, $5,000, over and above the ordinary rates to American ports, and as the vessel made five trips, he paid $25,000 additional insurance. That meant $25,000 out of the pockets of the consumers and the producers of this country.
The worst feature is the damage done to the reputation of the route.

In addition, my hon. friend will bear this in mind, that investigation can only be held by the Department of Marine and Fisheries for the purpose of finding out what takes place in the St. Lawrence. The department has no control over the captain's certificate. That must be dealt with by the board of trade in England. To show how careful these investigations held by Commander Spain were, let me point out that the results of his investigations have been confirmed in almost every instance by the board of trade in England. Ship masters have had their certificates taken from them or been suspended or reprimanded in conformity with

Commander Spain's report. I may add that I have had some experience of his investigations and have always found him most competent for the purpose. There is a line of steamships which has been coming to the St. Lawrence for the last twelve years-the Holme Line, of which Kennedy and McLean are the agents. These men exercise particular care in the choice of their captains, and the result has followed that there has not been a single accident to one of their steamers during all that period. My hon. friend should bear in mind also that the vessels which come to the St. Lawrence, with the exception of a few regular liners, are tramp steamers. They are under the control of masters who are not competent. Two thirds of them have not the requisite experience and capacity to guard against the difficulties attendant on river navigation. You have in the St. Lawrence, not only the difficulties connected with the shoals, rocks and reefs, but with the currents, which is one of the most serious difficulties you can meet in a river. In addition you have these other difficulties, resulting from the immense mass of iron deposits on both sides of the St. Lawrence, and in consequence of which you never can tell whether your compass is true or not, so that you have to exercise the greatest precaution because of the effect on the compass of these iron deposits. Therefore you require competent men, but all these difficulties can be overcome by the exercise of care and skill. The St. Lawrence can be made as safe a route as exists anywhere in the world. You have no difficulties there on that route that you have not got on the English channel and the river Mersey.	*

Before this item is passed,
I would like to make a few remarks, more ifi a general way than in the way of faultfinding with the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec, especially on the St. Lawrence, must agree that enormous interests are involved in the St. Lawrence route, and the question of insurance is one of the great questions in connection with that. I think it has been pointed out by the Minister of Justice that vessels are sent out to this country on which there is very serious moral hazard, and the insurance people of England, having enormous business all over the world, do not regard the insurance on the St. Lawrence route as they do that on the route, say to New York harbour. They will insure vessels going by the St. Lawrence route that they would not insure going by the New York harbour. As the minister has said, they are called, in many cases, tramp steamers. Thr-ough this abuse, the greatest possible injustice is done to the St. Lawrence route. I wish you to understand that the extra cost of $5,000 which, as has been pointed out, is put upon a vessel going out by the St. Lawrence route, is a discrimination of the exports of this country. We have been talking very learnedly about the transportation problem, but it has been left out of account that an enormous quantity of our breadstuffs, cattle and so on, exported from this country are diverted from the St. Lawrence route, largely because it has been made unpopular through the enormous loss made in connection with incoming vessels. The insurance companies are themselves to blame, for they are taking a moral hazard that an ordinary fire insurance company would not think of taking. Another matter that has been mentioned here is that of pilotage. Hon. members may think that in speaking of this, I am a crank on the union system. I understand that these pilots have been a most tyrannical union on the St.

Lawrence, that they have controlled elections, and that we ordinary politicians hardly dare to speak a word against their interest. I am glad that the lion. Minister of Justice has the courage to say that this is a matter that should have been taken hold ot by the government, and that should be taken hold of at once, for I do not see why any number of pilots, no matter how respectable, should demand consideration that interferes with the rights and interests of all the people of Canada. They should not be allowed to make the route unpopular which should be the great route, not only for Canada, but for the western states-as it would be if it were properly managed and made as popular as it might be made. I may say that I am very strongly in favour of unions;
I am in favour of workingmen uniting to maintain their own interests, but not for the purpose of opposing the interests of others. Therefore, no union of pilots on the St. Lawrence should be allowed that is opposed to the interests of all the people of Canada. The matter mentioned by the Minister of Justice is the key-note of the system. A vessel coming into the St. Lawrence is owned by fifty or sixty people, each having a very small interest. It reminds one of the adventurers of old times-each one of these owners takes an adventure. They send a vessel out well insured. If she makes a successful voyage, they make money ; and if the voyage is unsuccessful, the St. Lawrence route gets a black eye, and the insurers put their hands in their pockets and pay the loss. That is not a proper system of business-it is not business at all-it is brigandage. Therefore, thei-e should be a' united effort in every direction to discourage that kind of thing and every inducement given to encourage legitimate business. These magnificent steamers that come to our ports should be given every inducement to come. Just as we hold out inducements to internal navigation by making our inland waters free, so we should make the St. Lawrence route as free as possible, and particularly free from the exorbitant rates of insurance which hamper those who, like myself, endeavour to bring into this country every dollar's worth of goods we can by Canadian routes and over Canadian railways. When exports are forced to go by American routes, the effect is to make our imports by Canadian routes cost us more than we ought to pay, for the return cargo is the great matter, if you hope to make the St. Lawrence route successful. We must face the problems of how to make the St. Lawrence route all that both sides of the House desire it to be, to make it as safe as it can be made, to keep it free from political influences and political appointments, and to see to it that the public in England interested in shipping are kept as well posted as possible as to the real cause of the accidents that have tended to make our route unpopular.	:

It may be Interesting, since I have referred to the letter of Sir Alfred Jones, that I should read it to the committee. it coincides entirely with the suggestions that have been made. Sir Alfred Jones is quite au fait with what has taken place and, as will be seen, he is quite of the opinion that the accidents are not due to the conditions of the channel. The following is the letter :-
4 Sit. Mary Axe,
London, August 29, 1902.
My Dear Sir,-While your colleagues are across here we thought it was a good opportunity to take up a question as to the possibility of improvements in the St. Lawrence with a view to the benefit of the public and ourselves as we are large underwriters on our ships and cargo. We have seen Sir William Mulock and he informs us we had better put all the documents before you, therefore we beg to hand you copies of letters from our lighthouse department in Liverpool together with charts and suggestions. We think ourselves the suggestions made are all in the right direction, but if you will wire to our Montreal office they will send you a couple of our most experienced captains to confer with you as to the possibility of improvements all round. We feel sure that all the ministers are as equally anxious as ourselves to make the St. Lawrence route as popular as any other to the mainland. At present we are handicapped. The underwriters say we are in more risky navigation than northern ports of the United States, but it is nevertheless a fact that we have completed during the last three years about eighty voyages from Canada without a mishap. Therefore we are indignant that our ships should he charged eight per cent as against New' York three per cent, and it depends upon ourselves to convince the underwriters they are wrong. It will do no harm in trying to accomplish this to recognize in any way any deficiency we tray have had such as fog signals and buoys. Then can you make the draught of water a bit deeper and the turnings a little less difficult ? Anything we can do on this side-we are so deeply interested-we beg of you to command any assistance we can render.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) ALFRED JONES. Hon. James Sutherland,
Minister of Marine,
Ottawa.
This letter was duly acknowledged by my predecessor, and because of it the department asked the different captains whose names I have given to submit suggestions, which suggestions were made and some carried out, while others are Being carried out.

may mention that it was only in 189S that the harbour commissioners of Montreal began to force the pilots to submit to an examination as to their eyesight. Formerly they were only examined when they were admitted, or after they had attained the age of sixty-five. When I was a member of the Board of Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, I succeeded in having the by-laws amended and this new rule imposed on the pilots. I have been informed that some oculists-I will not mention names or places-are ready to give a certificate that the person is quite competent to be a pilot and that his eyesight is perfect, while another oculist, better aware of his duties, will refuse. subtopic: PENNY BANKS.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W.
S.	Fielding) introduced Bill (No. 198) respecting Penny Banks. He said : The object of this Bill, as its name implies, is the cultivation of thrift in small matters, the encouragement of small savings of a class not reached by the government savings bank. A year ago we had application from some public-spirited gentlemen of Toronto, who wished to obtain a special charter for the establishment of a bank of this character. We thought it better, however, if such banks were to be established, that it should be done under some general law which would apply to all established under similar circumstances. The gentlemen in Toronto very readily assented to that view, and we have prepared a Bill of a general character which will meet their case, and also, if they should arisef cases of a like character elsewhere. The design is that these institutions may be established by letters patent issued by the Governor in Council, and shall all come under the general rules laid down. It is intended that they shall not Mr. TAYLOR.
be money-making or money-lending institutions, but that they shall be entirely money-saving institutions. Indeed, it would not be too much to describe them as practically collecting agencies for the government savings bank. It is proposed that a small proportion of the funds they receive, 5 per cent, shall be held by the penny banks to meet the daily demands; but the balance shall be deposited with the government savings bank, and shall only be withdrawn when required by the depositors. The penny bank shall not require to have a capital; but the persons organizing it shall be required to have $10,000 as f guarantee of good faith. It is to be understood, not as a commercial undertaking, but rather as a benevolent institution, which will be established by churches and benevolent societies. For the money deposited in the government savings bank we propose to allow i per cent above the ordinary rate of interest, though the institution itself will not pay a larger rate of interest than the government savings bank. But to meet the expense of management, we propose to encourage the very worthy object of these gentlemen by paying to the bank i per cent higher interest than we pay to the ordinary depositor. If it should be found that * per cent would more than pay the cost of management, it will be reduced; but I do not anticipate that that will be the case. What I anticipate is that gentlemen establishing institutions of this character will do it for benevolent purposes, and will have to put their hands into their pockets and help to pay the expenses. They will be allowed to Invest their own guarantee fund in reasonably good securities, but the money of the depositors must be deposited in the government savings bank. These in brief are the main provisions of the Bill. We shall be very glad, when it reaches a later stage, to have any suggestions that may be offered to improve it. It has been prepared at the suggestion of the gentlemen in Toronto to whom I have referred; but we have thought it well to devise a system whereby, if similar savings banks should be started in other parts of the country, they would be brought under the operation of this Act.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: Is there any maximum amount that can be deposited ?

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: Yes, it must not exceed $300.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister if we have any coin in Canada equal to a penny, or what he means by a penny ?

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will consult the dictionary he will find that, although in England a
penny is described as a copper coin of a certain weight and character, it also means a small coin of any kind. In the United

States a small coin is called a penny, and the term is pretty well understood in that sense. In our decimal currency we have not anything which is technically called a penny ; but our Toronto friends who originated this proposal wished that the term should be adopted, and we have gratified their wish.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know of any place outside of Toronto where there are such banks ?

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: The Bill is general, and such a bank may be established anywhere; but the movement is led by these gentlemen in Toronto, who are anxious to establish such a bank.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: I think there are banks of this kind at other places which have been established longer than they have been in Toronto.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: But they have no charter. If they wished to have the stamp of authority, they would have to come under the provisions of this Bill.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: I suppose that such banks would not reach anything that could not be reached by the savings bank. There is no limit in the deposits of the savings banks ?

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: Yes, a dollar deposited at one time.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: I suppose these organizations might reach places which would not be reached by the government savings bank.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: It would be possible, but hardly likely. They will most likely be established in connection with some benevolent organizations in the large cities and towns.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: I understand that there is a description of penny bank or small savings bank which has come into vogue to some extent on the continent of Europe, and also in the United Kingdom, and which not only receives money on deposit, but lends money in small amounts to its own shareholders; and I am informed that there is a bank of that character established at the present time at L6vis. This proposed enactment, I gather from what the hon. gentleman has said, does not at all relate to institutions of that kind ?

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: Has the question suggested itself to the government as to whether or not banks of that kind should be given any legal status in this country ?

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext:
Yes ; several members of parliament, in conjunction with a gentleman who is officially connected with this House, recently called upon
me and described to me the bank which is now in operation at Levis, based on a similar principle to banks which exist in some European countries. I have promised that I will look into the matter, though I do not anticipate that we shall take any action upon it during the present session. But the banks to be established under this Bill will in no way conflict with such an institution, because these are not to be moneylending banks at all. The banks the hon. gentleman refers to, do lend money in a limited sphere.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: Only to their own shareholders.

subtopic: PENNY BANKS.
speechtext: Only to their own shareholders; and I understand that there is the very wholesome rule that the directors shall not lend to themselves. But this will in no way conflict with such institutions if later on we should decide to make provision for them.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair) moved that the House go into Committee of the Whole tomorrow, to consider the following resolution
1.	Resolved, that the government may aid the extension of the line of the Canadian Northern Railway Company from Grandview, the point where what is known as the Gilbert Plains branch of the said railway ends, to a point at or near Edmonton, a distance of about 620 miles, and also of the Prince Albert branch of the said railway from a .point 100 miles east of Prince Albert to Prince Albert, a distance of about 100 miles, by guaranteeing the principal and interest of the first mortgage bonds, debentures or other securities of the company to the extent of $13,000 per mile of the line, interest on the said bonds to be at the rate of three per cent per annum payable half-yearly, and the principal to be payable in 50 years.
2.	Resolved, that the said bonds, debentures or other securities shall be secured by mortgage forming a first charge upon the lines of railway so aided, and all property and franchises in connection therewith, and all revenues derived therefrom by the company ; provided that with respect to that portion of the said line from the end of the Gilbert Plains
branch to the westerly boundary of Manitoba, a distance not exceeding sixty-five miles, the said mortgage shall be a first charge to the extent of only $10,000 per mile, but shall also rank on the said portion next after the charges heretofore created ; provided also that the said mortgage shall be a charge next after a first charge of $13,000 per mile (to be created by the company) on that part of said Prince Albert branch.
3.	Resolved, that the said mortgage shall also form a charge next after the charges existing thereon upon all the lines and branch lines of railway of the company now in operation, and all property and franchises connected therewith. and all revenues derived therefrom by the company.
4.	Resolved, that the kind of securities to be guaranteed as aforesaid, and the forms thereof, and the form and terms of the mortgage securing them, and the form and manner of guarantee, shall be such as the Governor in Council approves of.
5.	Resolved, that upon the said guarantee being signed on behalf of the government, the government shall become liable for the payment of the principal and interest of the securities guaranteed, and the said payment shall be a charge upon the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
6.	Resolved, that the rates and tolls to be charged for the transfer and carriage of freight and passengers upon the lines of railway 30 aided and upon the lines owned by the Canadian Northern Railway shall be under the control of the Governor in Council or of such authority, commission or tribunal as is designated or constituted under any Act of the parliament of Canada for the regulation or control of the business of railways.
7.	Resolved, that the Governor in Council or any authority created ,by parliament for the purpose may also grant running powers over any portion of the lines hereby aided to any other line of railway upon terms considered equitable.
8.	Resolved, that it shall be unlawful for the Canadian Northern Railway to lease or sell any of its lines or any portion thereof to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or to amalgamate with the .said company or enter into any agreement with the said company whereby rates upon freight or passengers shall be pooled; but this provision shall not extend to traffic or running arrangements made with the assent of the Governor in Council.
9.	Resolved, that any money paid by the government of Canada under the guarantee herein provided for shall be held to be paid in discharge of the liability of the government, but not in discharge of the liability of the mortgage securing them ; and the money so paid shall be held to be still secured by the said securities and mortgage, and the government shall be subrogated in all the rights of the holders of the securities, the interest upon or the principal of which has been paid by the government, and the government shall in respect of all the moneys so paid be in all respects in the position of security holders in respect of whose securities default has been made in payment to the extent of the moneys paid by the government.
He said : I may say, Mr. Speaker, that his Excellency the Governor General having been apprised of the purpose of this motion, assents thereto and recommends it to the House.

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Last year we had a discussion with regard to scales to be adapted to threshing machines used in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. At the time I declared that I was almost sure that the weighing machine then in use did not meet the provisions of the Act which required that those scales should be inspected. Unfortunately that scale was not made according to law. Since then the owner of that scale, or somebody in lxis Interest, has been working on it in order to perfect it, and I am informed that as now manufactured it would be considered sufficient, but it is not yet in our possession. In the meantime, to prevent other difficulties winch have been experienced I understand for several years past, we Introduce this clause, which may be repealed by Order in Council as soon as a scale is found suitable to answer the purposes of the law, and gives satisfaction to the public. As the clause reads, in order to avoid any difficulty between the owners of threshing machines and the farmers, we have asked that an inspected scale he used so that when any difficulty arises between the owner of the grain and the owner of the threshing machine .in regard to the weight of the grain, the difficulty may be settled by check tests.

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I observe that the provisions of this enactment seem to be dependent upon some check established by the second subsection :	There are to
*be Check weights on a properly verified scale. It seems to me legislation of that kind may be found unworkable, in some instances at least. You are making the operation of the Act dependent upon an agreement between the two persons interested. What operations will the section have then ? Of course if the man who owns the threshing machine and the owner of the grain come to an agreement, we really do not want any legislation. But if they do not come to an agreement, I do not see how you can make much progress under this section, because the whole of the section is dependent apparently upon the check established by section 2, and that check is based upon an agreement between the two parties. Well, is not that rather unworkable in the only case in which you might find much occasion to apply it ?

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I have already explained the difficulty that arises when the farmer and the owner of the threshing machine do not agree. But even when they do agree, after the grain is threshed the farmer may begin to complain because there was no .weighing machine attached to the threshing machine, and I am told that judgments have been rendered by the courts sustaining the farmer in refusing to pay. In order to remedy that difficulty we adopt a machine as a temporary measure, and until we have a machine that will give satisfaction to both parties we have thought it best to introduce this legislation. But in order to give satisfaction both to the farmer and the owner of the machine, we have made provision that if at any time, at any hour of the day, either one of the parties is not satisfied that the scale is working properly, they may weigh by another scale, and the inspected scale is used to ascertain whether the weighing machine is working properly or not.

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If the statute meant what the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Bernier) seems to think it does I would be inclined to agree witli him, but I do not think it does. If the second clause said that either party would have the right to have the weights verified not less than four times, or six times, per day and at intervals of not less than an hour, or half an hour, you could work it out, but where you make it dependent upon the agreement of both parties I cannot see how you are going to work it out except where both parties actually- agree to that. The object of the statute is to effect a remedy in cases where the parties do not agree, where they are at arm's length. It does not seem that the statute carries out what the hon. minister has in his mind.

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: As I have already explained, this is only a temporary measure. If these people cannot agree, even when they make a bargain between themselves, I do not see how any law can oblige them to be satisfied, unless we can make provision that they shall have an opportunity to try or test the weights any time in the day. If they are willing they can test them twenty times in the day. Both parties will be interested in having correct weights, first, the farmer who has to pay and the owner of the threshing machine who has to receive the money. I have inquired what we can do in that direction and I have come to the conclusion that we had better not fix the number of times in a day that a test may be made.
