speechtext:
The movement was not started until the department had received complaints from people from the North-west Territories. As soon as these complaints reached the department we took measures to provide some remedy. One of our officers at Winnipeg, the inspector of weights and measures, informed the department that he was working on a machine which would be perfected in a short time. In order to ascertain if he was right or wrong, because he had occupied the dual position of inventor and inspector of his own machine, that gentleman came to Ottawa, and in presence of gentlemen from Manitoba and the Northwest Territories his machine was put into motion. As the inspector was the inventor of the machine he could not very well pass judgment on his own invention, and we submitted it to Mr. Fyfe, who is well known throughout the Dominion for his ability in this business. Mr. Fyfe was then a scale manufacturer in Montreal, and he is now our chief inspector of weights and measures. Mr. Fyfe stated in presence of the inventor that the machine was not perfect, as it could not be verified, and, if I remember aright, Mr. Magness admitted it. When I stated last year that I expected a machine would be ready for this season, it was on the representation of Mr. Magness, who told me that the machine would give satisfaction to everybody. When the machine had turned out not to be perfect, correspondence took place whether between Mr. Magness or the Globe Manufacturing Company, and the department. Mr. Fyfe contended that even if changes were made the scale could not be admitted to inspection and verification, and in order to show that the department had left nothing undone to give satisfaction to the people of the North-west, I may read the following letter, which the deputy minister wrote on November 11th last to a firm of lawyers in Winnipeg, with whom he had correspondence :
As to the machine submitted being capable of weighing correctly when operated at the proper speed, the chief inspector to whom this matter was referred states that he has no recollection of the necessity for the machine being run at any specified rate of speed being marked thereon, and that even had such been done he could not recommend the verification of any weighing machine that required to be operated at an indicated speed as an essential feature of its weighing correctly. The department has been most anxious that a suitable scale, for use with grain threshers, should be 132
constructed and is prepared to go aside from many less important features provided the essential provisions of the law and regulation be observed and that the scale is of a character to remove the difliculties complained of in. grain-producing districts. I may even go further and state that the services of the chief inspector will willingly be placed at the disposal of any person undertaking the production of such a scale. I hoped that the scale submitted would be of such a character, and my disappointment is certainly as great as that of the gentleman who placed it before the department for approval.
If the scale originally submitted has been changed as respects the objectionable features pointed out in my first letter, the department will be glad to have another scale passed upon by the chief inspector.
I may admit that the law is perhaps not perfect, but it will be beneficial to have it on the statute-book until such time as a new scale will be invented, in order to prevent the difficulties which have arisen in the past.

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I wish to point out to the minister, the importance of this matter to the farmers of Manitoba and the North-west. The owners of these threshing machines are farmers, and they do the threshing for their neighbours as well as for themselves. Instead of doing all this work by hand, as was formerly the system, the apparatus has developed, until now there is a machine to do all the work of loading into bags and keeping count of every bushel measured. This is now done automatically, and time and labour and expense are saved. If you remove this device from the threshing machines in the west, it will mean an increased cost on the present amount of crop of at least $1,000,000 more to the farmers of the west. I assert that without this machine they would have to pay at least $1,000,000 more to handle their crop. I have here a lengthy reply to the criticisms of Mr. Fyfe, and I will read one or two paragraphs of it which refer to this machine. I am well aware, as the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) stated, that we were invited to see the machine tested in the minister's office. I was present myself, when the weigher made and used on the J. I. Case threshing machine, was in the office. Their agent was here, and their machine was criticised, and they, the officials of the department, explained all they had to do to manufacture it, showing how the bearings should be hardened in order that it might pass the inspection. Let me say here that there appears to be some misunderstanding about this matter. The minister states that Mr. Magness is the inventor of the machine, but I understand from the machine men in Winnipeg that two young men, Messrs. Leitch and Drummond, of the Globe works, are the inventors of this machine. I know that they are the men who are making it and are working on it. I quote the following from the inspector's report of March 19th, page 42 [DOT].



Referring to the inspector's report of March 19th, on page 42, it is admitted that the machine does not balance either with or without the load. As previously explained, about seven pounds of the load is required to he in the bucket before the machine is brought into equilibrium, but this in no way interferes with the accuracy in weighing of the machine. The principle of balancing is not at all applicable to this machine, as in actual work, it operates so rapidly that there would not be time for any one to inspect the weights after the predetermined weight of grain has been deposited in the bucket. In threshing with ordinary grain the bucket would fill and empty grain twenty or thirty times per minute, so that there would be no interval of time after the bucket has filled, for a farmer or any person else to inspect it for the purpose of ascertaining whether it correctly balanced with the load or without the load, but if any farmer, whose grain has been threshed, has doubts about the accuracy of the weighing, he can always test by weighing one or more discharges of the bucket on this platform scale.
The makers of this weigher considered the small sketch prepared by the inspector, which you kindly forwarded to them and, which, he states, ' would convey to them the groundwork of success in developing and perfecting of their grain weigher ' ; but, after carefully considering this sketch and with every desire to improve their machine by the utilization of Mr. Fyfe's idea, they are forced to the conclusion that the adoption of his ideas would not only not improve their machine, but would render it absolutely useless as a grain weigher. In this sketch Mr. Fyfe employs four more knife edge bearings that are in use in the Standard Grain Weigher, and he expresses the opinion that, if this sketch is adopted, it will weigh accurately and meet all the requirements of the Weights and Measures Act, but, in his subsequent report of April 1st, on page 52 of the report, he contradicts this by the statement, ' In my opinion, the use of a knife scale for the purpose intended is impracticable, as it is impossible to weigh correctly on account of the vibration of the machine in threshing.' In penning this last quoted sentence, he has evidently forgotten that, in his report of March 27th, on page 50 of the report, he states ' The nucleus of a good serviceable scale is embodied in the machine presented for admission.' In his report of April 1st, page 21, he speaks of his long experience as a scale manufacturer and of his employment by capitalists to investigate and report on patent weighing machines, and follows up with the gratuitous statement that ' the makers of the machine in question have designed it from a purely mechanical standpoint, without regard, not only to the Weights and Measures requirements, but without regard to the demands of science in the application of leverage and gravity.' The inventors of the Standard Grain Weigher are practical men, who, we venture to say, know quite as much of the demands of science in the application of leverage and gravity as Mr. Fyfe does. Not only this, but the machine in question has been submitted to the inspection of one of the largest scale manufacturers in the United States, who has given it his unqualified approval after careful examination, not of fifteen minutes, but an examination and test extending over several days. The makers of this device have given special study to the principles involved in the building of weighing machines, with a full knowledge of all the surrounding *circumstances1 and the conditions under which Mr. STEWART.
it has to be operated, advantages which Mr. Fyfe has not enjoyed.
If this machine or any other weighs accurately, why should it not be admitted us a special weighing machine in this business ? There is nothing that it weighs but grain, and when the threshing machine is worn out, it is thrown on the scrap heap.

1 may say to my hon. friend that I would not have brought the name of Mr. Magness into the discussion if it had not been for the fact that the department was made aware that he was the inventor of the machine. On the 3rd of June, last year, he wrote the following letter :
I wrote Mr. C. Higman on May 27th, that it was important to me that he should make his report on the Standard Grain Weigher presented by me to the department, so that I could get a letter saying it was accepted or otherwise. I know it is necessary that I should forward a full sized machine for the standard room, also photo cut for circular. I intend to send one of the first batch made, but it takes some time to get the parts in quantities.
A party here is anxious to buy the Canadian right to build them, but I have no proof it has been accepted.
An early reply will greatly oblige.
Later on Mr. Magness, who was given every means to perfect his machine, was asked by the department to come down here with it, and was informed that he could not be both the inventor and the inspector of the machine. On the 17th of June, a letter was written to him, from which I take the following extract :
I have serious doubts as to the advisability of your being connected in any way, with the manufacture and sale of this thresher scale. 1 am not aware of the exact position in which you will stand at the time this scale will be placed upon the market. While it will be a great boon to the people of the west to have a properly inspected scale for use with the threshers, and while the matter is one in which the department is much interested, I am of the opinion that it would be most objectionable for you, as an inspector of weights and measures to be connected with its manufacture or sale.
We bad no correspondence with any other gentleman in reference to that scale than Mr. Magness himself. After he received our letter of the 17th of June, he wrote to Mr. Gerald, the Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue, on the 10th of the same month, as follows :
In reply to your letter of the 7th ult., I beg leave to say that I hold a third interest in the Globe Machine Company, who own the Standard Grain Weigher ; after my return from Ottawa our solicitor, T. J. Mathers, who is also solicitor for the Department of Justice, advised me to transfer my interest to him to hold in trust for me, which I have done, therefore, my name will not appear in any form when the company's Act of incorporation appears in the Manitoba ' Gazette.'
I intend to sell my interest in Canada at the first opportunity for anything like a fair price, which I cannot get now until the machine ha3 proved itself in the field, which we will do this

fall ; then I know there will be parties ready to buy.
On the 7th of October last, Mr. Maguess again wrote to the deputy minister, as follows :	i ^
Replying to your letter of the 7th of June, 1902, asking me to define my position re ' Standard Grain Weigher,' and my private letter replying thereto, I wish now to supplement or rather replace that letter :
I, therefore, beg to notify you that I have disposed of all my Canadian interest in tha*t grain weigher, and am neither directly nor indirectly connected with its sale or in the profits arising therefrom.
I trust this may relieve the department of all the anxiety and annoyance my former connection in this matter may have engendered.
After we had this correspondence we wrote to the Globe Manufacturing Company, which I presume has supplied my hon. friend with a report and with the exchange of correspondence between Mr. Fyfe and the gentleman connected with that firm. The following message was sent to the Globe Manufacturing Company, Winnipeg, Manitoba :
Ottawa, May 29, 1903.

subtopic: O. HIGMAN,

speechtext: There you have official information from the department, with the knowledge of the hon. minister, that the officer, who had for many years been the only chief inspector of weights and measures in Canada, notified these gentlemen who were interested in this machine that it had been admitted to verification. Subsequently that machine was brought down here to be inspected by the Manitoba and territorial members, and was found to be correct. But at a later date some new light apparently came on the department, a new light had arisen in Israel in the person of Mr. Fyfe, who went back on the statement of Mr. Higman, and gave a lot of technical reasons to show why the machine was not correct. He subsequently, in a communication which I have not before me, reflects qu the members from Manitoba and the North-west, who advocated

this machine. Could they have done otherwise when they had the report of the highest official of the department that it was perfect ? Why does not Mr. Fyfe reflect on that official ? We have not beard the hon. minister say why that official was discharged or what he is doing now. But we have a verification of this machine-not by either one of these technically instructed men, men who were accustomed to see threshing done by the flail and weighed by the steelyard, and who know nothing about threshing as it is done on a large scale-but by farmers who have used it. I have letters from many of them, showing that this machine has done perfect work, and I would put their evidence every day against the evidence of men who have only technical knowledge. Another objection is that Mr. Magness was interested in the patent and should not be inspector. Well, if that were the case, it was the duty of the minister to dismiss him. As a matter of fact, I know that Mr. Magness had nothing to do with the patent. It is true that he acquired an interest in it, and if that was contrary to the rules of the department, the minister should have at once discharged him. I submit that this Bill should stand over, and if necessary we should have some farmers brought down here to give evidence under oath who have tested this machine. Ten or fifteen can be brought, and I think that any hon. gentleman will take their opinion, based on a practical test, in preference to that of Inspector Fyfe, with all his great ability.

subtopic: O. HIGMAN,
speechtext: I have said already that Mr. Higman has never been chief inspector. I do not sec why so much objection should be raised to this provision of the law, because it is only intended to allow the use of some machine. We are bound to do something, and, in order to enable Mr. Magness, or the Globe Manufacturing Company, or anybody else, to have the machine under their control or any other machine brought into use, we are introducing legislation in order that we may permit the use of any of these machines. Otherwise, they could not be legally used, unless we changed the whole law. This is a law of exceptions, it is a temporary law. I think that my hon. friend may be led into error in saying that Mr. Fyfe was discourteous to the hon. members from Manitoba and the North-west Territories. I do not so interpret his letter. The members from Manitoba and the North-west Territories were anxious that this machine should be supplied in order to be ready for last fall. What would be the result, even if farmers from Manitoba and the North-west were brought here to show that the machine was working well ? I do not say that it is not working well. But what I say is that, as the law is now it cannot be inspected ; and, in order to remedy that, and not to destroy the law entirely, I am now introducing a Bill by

subtopic: O. HIGMAN,
speechtext:
I think that the evidence brought before the committee by the discussion that bas taken place shows one thing very clearly-that through a spat, or misunderstanding, or whatever you call it, amongst the officers of the department over which the hon. gentleman presides, the farmers may suffer, or, rather, not the farmers, but those who have done five million dollars worth of work not a dollar of which they can legally collect for. And the correspondence brought down contains a letter from the chief inspector which was a gross piece of impertinence to the members of this House from Manitoba and the North-west Territories. The responsibility for that, if the truth were known, rested upon the minister himself and his officers, for the desire of the members from Manitoba and the North-west was not that any particular machine should be adopted-not at all. It was the minister and his officers that brought this machine to the attention of the members from Manitoba and the North-west. In order to relieve the situation, the members from Manitoba and the North-west were prepared to accept it. And then to have these imputations cast upon them by an employee, a man who we are paying, decidedly too much. But while he thought he was reflecting upon the members from Manitoba and the North-west, he was reflecting upon his own minister and his predecessor. As has been shown by the correspondence, Mr. Higman verified this machine. The minister, in his speech a little while ago said that Mr. Higman had done this without authority. But I have here the correspondence. Under date of [DOT]Tune 3rd, Mr. Magness writes to the deputy minister :
I wrote Mr. O. Higman on May 27, that it was important to me that he should make his report on the standard grain weigher presented by me to the department.
And, in the reply of the deputy minister, you will find this paragraph :
I will bring the matter ot thresher scale to Mr. Higman's attention as soon as he returns to Ottawa, and the stereo should he sent in as soon as possible.
Does the minister wish the committee to believe that Mr. Higman made the report without any suggestion from any other officer ? Was it not more likely that the matter was brought to his attention as the deputy minister said, and that, in pursuance of instructions given him, he inspected the machine and made the report read by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary).

And then, this man was brought in from Montreal and pitchforked over the heads of men who, I believe, and I am sure the majority of the officers of the department believe, were his superiors in their qualifications for dealing with this matter. And this man, when he comes in. says : I am going to do this thing myself ; I am going to have a measuring machine that will measure which weighs about five hundred pounds and will hang on the top of the thresher twenty feet high. And the members from Manitoba and' the North-west Territories whose constituents are suffering through this delay and this quarrel in the department, are supposed to stand by and wait.

They have within reach an article that will meet the requirements of law, which can be made by any manufacturer without rpyalty, and yet they aje trying to force upon the farmers of the North-west an inferior machine that is patented and exclusive property of one manufacturer.

subtopic: O. HIGMAN,
speechtext: Who introduced that machine to the attention of members of the House ?

subtopic: O. HIGMAN,
speechtext: Mr. Magness.

subtopic: O. HIGMAN,
speechtext: Not at all, it was the Minister of Inland Revenue.

subtopic: O. HIGMAN,
speechtext: No, we must not be mistaken. I have the whole correspondence here. Mr. Magness informed me that he was perfecting a machine which he thought might be inspected, and after he had submitted it to me, Mr. Higman, who I repeat has never been a chief inspector of weights and measures, asked Mr. Magness to come down with this machine in order to have it tested by a man of experience. Before that test was made, I presume the members of the Northwest had examined it and found it satisfactory ; still when we decided to inspect the machine, we called in the services of a man of experience. The objection is not against the machine itself. The real difficulty is to devise some means by which the farmers and the owners of the threshing machines may settle their difficulties without the intervention of a court. What would be the use of having a scale inspected which mighe be set aside by a court of justice, and thus multiply the expenses ? We have done the best we could, and now we have come to the conclusion that, pending the time when we get a machine that will meet the requirements of the law, we had better introduce this legislation, which I hope will give relief to a certain extent.

subtopic: O. HIGMAN,
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, so long as we arrive at the desired end, I do not know that we need care just by what particular road the end is reached. I think the Bill will meet the object which we all have in view. It indirectly legalizes this machine which we are discussing, or any other machine on which the threshers and farmers may agree. I trust, therefore, that the Bill may pass. But I wish to endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) in regard to the attitude and action of this officer of the Inland Revenue Department. I am disposed to agree entirely with the minister, that Mr. Fyfe is an exceedingly clever gentleman ; my own opinion is that he is too clever by half. I have read with some care the report that he has made regarding this automatic weighing device, and also the document that is at present in the possession of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Stewart) answering the objections made by Mr. Fyfe. In one paragraph of this report which has already been read to the House, he suggests that he has recommended one machine, and I would point out to the minister that in that ma-

chine which Mr. Fyfe himself suggests, there are some of the same defects that he contends exist in the other machine which he condemns. The paragraph of Mr. Fyfe's report which is complained of is the following
The members who are fighting the battle for the ' Grain Threshing Scale ' makers, do not seem to see that they are unknowingly occupying a false position, opposed to their own interests and to the interests of those they represent. They have within reach an article that will meet the requirements of the law, which can be made by any manufacturer, without royalty, and yet they are trying to force upon the farmers of the North-west an inferior machine that is patented and exclusive property of one manufacturer.
The members from Manitoba and the Northwest may perhaps be super-sensitive, but I am bouud to say that I entirely agree with what has been said by my hon. friend from Macdonald with regard to this paragraph. Of course, we all know that there are men who think they can run other peoples' businesses better than those people themselves. I suppose it has always been the case that there are certain members of the civil service at Ottawa who think that they can govern this Dominion a great deal better than parliament, and that it would be a great deal better if parliament were abolished and the government were left In their own hands. That may be perfectly true, but so long as the people, under the constitution, elect representatives to frame legislation, I think it would be well for every minister of the Crown to see that the officers under him do not cast such reflections upon members of this House as are cast by this paragraph. So long as we are sent here as representatives of the people, I beg to say that we are under no obligation or necessity to put up with the insolence of language which this officer introduces in his report.

speechtext:
The amendment is in the twentieth line in which the words ' not exceeding customary and fair commercial rates for similar work or supplies in similar quantities ' are substituted for these words in the Act of 1893 ' not exceeding that which would be charged for such printing ' at the Printing Bureau. Under the Statute of 1S93 authority was given to the government to Mr. SCOTT.
have the printing which was required for the Intercolonial Railway and Prince Edward Island Railway done elsewhere than at the Printing Bureau, and a provision was made in the Statute of 1893 that the cost of such printing should not exceed the cost at the Printing Bureau in Ottawa. That was found to be impracticable and as a result the work was always done at the printing offices in the maritime provinces ,at a cost exceeding the cost at which the work could be done at the Printing Bureau, and the King's Printer, Dr. Dawson, invariably certified the accounts as fair and reasonable. This went on from 1893 until November, 1902, when the Auditor General discovered that the certificates were not according to law, and as a result you will find a very protracted correspondence that was exchanged between the Printing Bureau and the Auditor General at page W-377 of the Auditor General's Report. The very minute the Auditor General objected to this certificate given by the King's Printer, the matter was referred to the Department of Justice, and we were obliged to report that the certificate was not sufficient under the statute, and that, while the custom had become almost equivalent to law, as objection had been taken by the Auditor General, there was nothing to do but to conform to the strict enforcement of the statute. As a result it has been found necessary to give statutory effect to the custom which has prevailed for years, and to substitute for the words in the old statute that at a cost not exceeding that which would be charged for .such printing at the Printing Bureau ; these words ' at customary and fair commercial rates for similar work or supplies in similar quantities.'

the Printing Bureau and what portion is done elsewhere.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY.
speechtext: I could not tell that very well at present. We are continuing the practice about on the same basis in that regard as it has been continued for a long period of years. The arrangement which my hon. friend the Hon. Minister of Justice says was made in 1893 was a well considered arrangement. It was reported upon and the views of the King's Printer were had on the subject. He argued the question, presented the reasons pro and con, the Auditor General agreed and it was submitted to the Governor in Council and approved of, and from that time down till November of last year the scale was continued uniformly and on the same basis and the printing was done at the various points along the route of the railway. The present action results from the view which the Auditor General took. I have not, in my mind, at the present moment, an accurate idea as to' what portion of the printing is done in the Bureau and what portion outside. I would not like to state my view because I might fall short or exceed the fact, but I have no accurate idea of what portion of the printing is done in the Bureau or as to the difference between the charges, but the charges are based upon the rate which was adopted in 1893, and which has been uniformly continued for nine or ten years. I do know but that it is quite impossible to do a considerable portion of the work here. The distance is so great, and the necessity of sending the work back and forth for correction and so on, makes it impossible to do the work here with despatch. There are at present enough delays without needlessly increasing them. No public interest suffers by this. I would think that the clause which was decided upon after being well considered by the responsible and independent officers of the government in 1893, might very well be passed, as it is in this Bill.

As respects the work done on tickets, he says :
As I have pointed out in my annual reports the Bureau is overcrowded with work during the session of parliament and there is not room enough in the building for the hands required. rate of wages ? Is it the average rate ? If so, how is that average rate to be ascertained ? I would suggest that the city of Ottawa be included, or else that only one city be taken. As a matter of fact, you cannot get the average of three cities, because there would be no fair basis. If there is to be any real attempt to carry out the idea of this clause, it should be amended by adding that this rate shall be ascertained by the fair wage officer once every year or once every two years ; otherwise there is no way of being sure what is the current rate. Now, I am aware what this question involves, because it has been discussed lately. It is claimed that the men in the Bureau are getting higher wages than those which prevail in Montreal, in Toronto, or in Ottawa. It is claimed, without any proof being brought forward, that they are getting more than the union rate of wages in those cities. Most people who know very little about trades organizations maintain that a union fixes a rate of wages which every body must get-a maximum rate. In the printing business this is altogether wrong. The union only sets a minimum rate. I believe the minimum rate in Montreal is $12 a week. The current rate for competent men is far above that. There are plenty of men in the city of Montreal to-day getting twice what the union calls for. In the city of Toronto, I believe the minimum rate is $12.50. The current average rate would be about $15. Whether the minister recognizes the fact or not, the ascertaining of tile rates in either of these cities is a very complicated question. In the Bureau at the present time there is a flat rate for every man, whether he is competent or not. The government have put in force that very principle which we object to in trades organizations, that a flat rate should be enforced, that ability should not be worth more than non-abilitv. At the present time the rate is higher than the minimum rate in either Montreal or Toronto. At the same time, if this provision is to go into effect, it should be understood whether it is the current average rate or the current minimum rate that is to be fixed, and some machinery should be provided for ascertaining the rate. The rates of wages in Montreal and Toronto have been gradually rising. In Toronto they are lower to-day than they should be, because two years ago the employers and employees signed a scale covering three years, and, although they are loyally standing by that agreement, yet, as a matter of fact there are very few men getting as low a rate as the agreement calls for. Therefore, I am sure that the minister will see that it is by no means definitely settled what the rates are in those two cities. Then there is this other fact, that the two cities differ materially. I believe that that is a very fair way of settling things. We have no trouble whatever with our men. The men employed in the office with which I am connected are all union men. Their wages are fixed in the way I have pointed out, and I do not see why the same process should not be followed here. The King's Printer occupies the position of employer in any office where union men are employed. I believe that the way I have pointed out is a very fair way and that my hon. friend is taking a wrong standpoint. Let the men and the employers come together as closely as they can. One reason why there is no trouble between employers and printers is because we have daily relations together. I suppose that I see the men employed in my office ten times a day, I am glad to see them and they are not sorry to see me. We have one man who has been with us for twenty-five years, and who is counted as one of ourselves. My hon. friend is taking a wrong stand in asking for an outside party. Although I recognize the ability of some of the men in the Labour Bureau, I think that the best and most rational way is to have the employers and employees settle wages and their business relations together. That is what is done in Montreal. If my hon. friend will do us the pleasure to come and see us, he will find harmony and amity and good will between employers and employees. PATENT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is this legislation founded upon legislation in any other country, or is it entirely new ?

subtopic: PATENT ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
It is practically identical with legislation which has been adopted in England recently. Mr. Lloyd Wise has worked out the problem, has submitted his conclusions to the parliament of Great Britain and has recommended them to us. I may say that the reason why this legislation seems to be necessary at the present time is that the Supreme Court decided that a patentee, being prepared to supply the goods in Canada on demand was not sufficient justification for the life of a patent. Until that decision of the Supreme Court, the patent officer had always held and the courts had also held that if a patentee was ready to supply the goods hut did not manufacture them his patent remained valid. After the decision of the Supreme Court tn December last in the case of Powell vs. Griffin, I think it was, it is evident that the practice of the department and these rulings of the courts were not sustained, and today, if the patentee does not actually manufacture or produce the article in Canada within a certain time his patentee becomes null and void. There are classes of patents under which it is practically impossible for the patentee to produce or manufacture the article in Canada. One of these classes refers to an article of great construction, a class of articles or things of which practically only one or two would be constructed in the country. For instance there is a graving dock or a lift lock, such as has recently been constructed on the canal, or an elevator, things that are patentable hut the use of which is very rare, and to require that a patent shall expire if it has not been made use of and the thing has not been constructed in the country is certainly an in-

justice and is destroying the object and aim of the patent law of encouraging inventors to invent these things and get them patented. This Bill provides machinery by which, when the patentee has such a patent as that, he can apply to the commissioner and protect himself without actually constructing the thing or getting it constructed because he makes provision by which, if it is required in the country, it can be constructed, and this section puts into the hands of the commissioner of patents the entire control of the terms and conditions under which construction shall be carried out under a reasonable and fair basis to both the patentee and the person who wishes to use the patent. There is another class of patents which would come under this provision and that is the class called patents of processes, for instance, a patent for using a chemical process in manufacture. This is a class of patents which cannot be used unless the industry in which these processes are supposed to be useful is carried on in the country. If it is carried on and if the people who are carrying it on desire to use a patent such as this, then and then only, would the patentee be in a position to put the process into operation or sell his patent. Now, this thing is entirely out of the control of the patentee and it seems to me that it would be unreasonable that this patent should lapse and become void under such circumstances. That patent would also come under the provisions of this section; and enable the patentee to apply to come in under that clause and this enables the commissioner to control the arrangement under which he would retain his patent and provide proper facilities in the country for its use.

speechtext: This requires some explanation. A case came before the department not long ago of an application made for an extension of the time within which to manufacture in the country. It has been usual in the department, where there was no opposition filed, to grant such extensions of time on the mere statement of the applicant. In this case there was an opposition, the case was discussed and the opposing views were represented before the commissioner. Eventually the case was referred to the Department of Justice, and that department gave a written opinion that no extension of time should be granted unless valid arguments were given in the application, and unless it was shown that it was absolutely proper to grant the extension, and the patentee was prevented by circumstances beyond his control from manufacturing within the specified time. This was an entirely new practice, but, with the written opinion of the Department of Justice to that effect, it is understood we must change our practice, and, for the future, only grant extensions of time when such cause is shown. It has been the practice for people to come asking for extension of time within a week or two of the date of expiry of their term. In many cases, where the patentee lives at a distance, it would be physically impossible for him to have his application returned with an explanation of what was required, and come back within the time required for proper consideration. We, therefore, ask that the commissioner be allowed until the 1st of January next to concede such application, even if the concession is granted a little while after the time specifically allowed. We believe that by the 1st of January the new practice in the department will be well known and all such applicants will have an opportunity of making their application well within that period. This is a mere concession in consequence of the change of the practice in the department.

On section 3,
Every owner of animals and every breeder of or dealer in animals, and every one bringing animals into Canada, shall, on perceiving the appearance of infectious or contagious disease among the animals owned by him or under his special care, give immediate notice to the minister and to the nearest veterinary inspector of the Department of Agriculture, of the facts discovered by him as aforesaid.
2. Any veterinary surgeon practising in Canada shall, immediately on ascertaining that an animal is labouring under an infectious or contagious disease, give similar notice to the minister and to the nearest veterinary inspector.
3. Every person neglecting to give notice as required by this section shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
Does this section affect animals in transit through Canada ?
_ The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. Yes, if an animal passing through Canada in transit, or at the time of entry, has a contagious or infectious disease, notice must be immediately given to the Minister of Agriculture and the nearest veterinary inspector of the department, of that fact. The old Act required that notice should be given to the Minister of Agriculture, but not to the nearest veterinary inspector.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Does it apply to American export cattle going through in bond, and which are shipped by way of Dominion ports ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: There are a great many cattle coming and going through Canada. It seems to me that these cattle should be subject to inspection and if there is any disease that the provisions of the Act should be applied.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: These cattle will be subject to this provision and if disease is found amongst them the owner must immediately notify the Minister of Agriculture and the nearest veterinary inspector. My hon. friend asks whether it would apply to animals in bond. That is a legal question that I would not like to give an opinion upon, but it likely would. Animals in bond are not in bond as far as contagious diseases are concerned.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Will the government have an inspector at Toronto for the purpose of examining and reporting upon these cattle, because the parties owning them, if the animals are affected by disease, would not be likely to report ? In that case will some official notify the minister ? The person in charge of these cattle will not be likely to give that notice.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The railways are obliged to give notice to the department.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Is there an inspector at all ports where American cattle come in ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We know that this trade only applies to certain ports and at these ports we have inspectors. The customs collectors are bound to call a veterinarian in any case of suspicion, but since the quarantine arrangement was made between us and the United States we have not inspectors at all ports.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
Are the cattle which come through in bond and which are fed in Toronto, inspected on the frontier, or only when they come to Toronto, or are they in-



spected at all ? The present system of feeding this cattle at Toronto is a most dangerous one. We have little opportunity to know whether these American animals are free from disease or not. They are fed and watered in the Toronto yards, and then young cattle are taken into the same pens and purchased there and distributed throughout Ontario. It is in my opinion the most dangerous thing in connection with our cattle trade. It is, I should think, impossible to know when diseased American cattle may come upon the scene.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: These United States cattle coming through in bond are all certified at the point of starting by the United States inspectors as being sound for export. They are allowed out in the pens at Toronto just like our own cattle and they are watched by the railway authorities who are obliged to report in case of disease. We must remember that this quarantine arrangement is only in existence so long as the United States is a healthy country, and when disease appeared in the New England states a short time ago we closed our frontier against New England cattle. We would do the same in case there was disease in the Western states. This quarantine arrangement has been in existence for six years and there lias not been a single instance where the disease was traced to these cattle.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: It is a great pity that these American cattle cannot be examined before they cross the frontier. It would be a most unfortunate thing should disease break out in our country, because the result would be that we could not ship our cattle at all, and as we have no dead meat trade our cattle business would be paralyzed. Too much care cannot be taken in this matter. There is no way iu which disease can be so easily introduced as by the existing arrangement.- I trust that the minister will take every precaution.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I wish to emphasize what my hon. friend (Mr. Gilmour) has said in reference to this. It would be most lamentable if disease were introduced into Canada by these cattle passing through iu bond. The farmers of Ontario buy their Stockers on the Toronto market, and if our animals should catch disease in these pens our whole cattle trade would be destroyed. I would like to impress upon the minister that there should be some inspection of these American cattle at the Toronto yards.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Does the minister know that all these cattle are inspected at the point of embarkation.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: They have to be certified by the United States authorities.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: But not by the Canadian authorities.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: No, We have a mutual arrangement by which we accept United States inspection and they accept ours; we having the same privileges to send cattle in bond to the United States as they have through Canada. No one would be more willing than I to safeguard our cattle.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I know that.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I am perfectly satisfied that there is no danger because there is no disease in these states.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: When the minister says there is no disease in these states, it must be remembered that it is hard to tell where these cattle come from to Chicago. They may be from Texas, Mexico or a great many other states. I do not know whether these cattle are disembarked at other places than Toronto or Montreal, but it would seem to me that it would be most desirable that they should be fed and watered at some other point than the Toronto stock yards, even if it cost some expense to the country.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: These cattle could not come from Texas or Mexico

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I suppose that is so, but at all events they come from a very wide territory surrounding Chicago.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes. The hon. gentleman mentioned Texas and Mexico, but these are countries which are infected with disease and we do not allow their cattle to come in at all. The United States authorities themselves do not allow cattle to pass from Mexico through New Mexico and Texas north of a line whch runs somewhere near the boundary of Missouri, and which is known as the Texas fever line.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: There is danger all the same. Would the minister think it would be useful to have an isolated yard, for the purpose of treating the cattle as they come through ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I appreciate the suggestion of the hon. gentleman, and shall be glad to. look into the matter and see if any further safeguard can be thrown around that trade. But I would point out that this particular section only emphasizes the point which the hon. gentleman made, that when any animal is known to be diseased, the information with regard to it must be immediately sent to the minister, and to the nearest veterinary inspector.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Then, I understand that one government has no check on the other with reference to these contagious diseases of cattle ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We are constantly communicating, and keeping each other informed. We have no check

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: except the honour of a great country, which has pledged itself to do certain things.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman not think that the United States has an advantage over Canada in that regard ? It is more to their advantage.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I would not like to say that we cannot depend on the honour of the United States government as well as they can depend on ours. Judging from the experience of the department in the past, I think we can do that.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister how this Act varies in this particular from previous Acts ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: This section requires the parties to inform the nearest official of the department in addition to the minister, so that prompt action may be taken. That is the difference between this Act and the old one.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: What is the meaning of the two words ' every person ' in subsection 3 ? Do they apply only to the owner, the breeder, the dealer and the veterinary surgeon 1 It seems to me to be a very broad expression, one which would include myself as well as the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Gifmour), so that we would be liable to the penalty if we failed to report to the nearest veterinary surgeon. I think the wording of the clause, if read carefully, means that and nothing else.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: No. If the hon. gentleman reads it carefully, he will see that it applies to every person neglecting to give notice as required by this section. It only applies to the people defined by this section.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: That may be the meaning of the minister, but the language would not strictly convey that idea. I think it would be unfair to make a private individual liable to a penalty of $200, particularly when he would get no compensation for the trouble he was going to.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The wording of the section does not mean that at all.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Put in the words ' having knowledge of disease,' and I think they would meet the case.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: That section is certainly altogether too wide. As the hon. minister knows, a good many men who are engaged in veterinary work to-day are not experts, and have no knowledge of what diseases are. Many owners certainly have not that knowledge.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Suppose I consult a veterinary about some animals, and lie tells me that they are not diseased, and on a later inspection I find that they are ; what then V

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: In the interest of the public we must insist that owners, on perceiving the appearance of infectious disease amongst their animals, shall notify the department. Of course, if they do not recognize that it is an infectious disease, they would not be liable to the penalty. There is no doubt of that under the wording of the Act.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
I am quite in accord with the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram) in protecting an innocent veterinary surgeon. Take the case of anthrax. I know that it is a very difficult matter for good medical men to determine a case of anthrax in a human being. It is not at all unusual for them to take the blood or some part of the flesh and have it analyzed by such a man ias Professor Ellis, of Toronto, to determine whether it is anthrax or not. It is not easy in many cases to determine whether a disease is infectious or not, and in a case of that kind it is rather hard for a man to be subject to a penalty of $200.
The MINISTER OF [DOT]AGRICULTURE. A penalty of that kind would be only imposed by the court upon a person who was found to be guilty. Such a case as the hon. gentleman mentions would afford a just reason for not imposing the penalty. It is not imposed on the arbitrary will of some autocrat ; it is imposed on evidence of the guilt of the party.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: It seems to me that the language of subsection 3 would be more effective if it were made to read, ' every owner of animals and every breeder of or dealer in animals, and every one bringing animals into Canada shall, on becoming aware of infectious or contagious disease,' &c. I think that would make it a little stronger and better.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
I might state to the hon. gentleman that the the words he takes exception to are copied verbatim out of the old Act. We took the old Act and changed it as little as possible.
I preferred to abide by the wording of the old Act, which has been in existence seventeen or eighteen years without any difficulty arising.
On section 9,
Every person who, without lawful authority or excuse, digs up or causes or allows to be dug up the buried carcass of au animal which has died or is suspected of having died from infectious or contagious disease, or which has been slaughtered as diseased or as suspected

of disease, shall, for every such offence, incur a penalty not exceeding ono hundred dollars.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Why make the penalty only one hundred under this clause when it is two hundred under the previous clause ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: It is that way in the old Act, and I have no objection to make it two hundred. I move that it be made $200.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: This clause should go further. It should be made punishable for a man even to bury the carcass of an animal which has died of an infectious disease. Take the case of anthrax. If you bury an animal which has died of anthrax, you plant the disease in the ground, and animals grazing there will be sure to contract it.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Under our regulations, which have the force of law, animals which have died of anthrax must be burnt.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Many people see the statutes who do not see the regulations.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The regulations are sent broadcast throughout the country, far more generally than are the statutes. Section 29 of this Act empowers the Governor in Council to make the necessary regulations.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Will a penalty for breaking the regulation be imposed as for breaking the Act.?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
Exactly.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 10,

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: This is to prevent the offering of infected animals for sale. The wording of the old Act is changed so as to enable an officer to seize and examine an animal suspected of being infected with contagious disease. Therefore, I move that the words ' Governor in Council,' in thS third line and in the seventh line on page three, be struck out and the word ' minister ' inserted.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Better say * Minister of Agriculture.'

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: That is provided for in the interpretation clause. Wherever the word ' minister ' is used it means the Minister of Agriculture.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
I think it is a little dangerous to pass this section just as it is. I do not know whether the minister has considered how this will work out in the actual enforcement of the Act. Of course we are here to make the law as practical as we can, and to make it easy of enforcement. I would suggest to him that it would be better if we should leave this enforcement to the ' mayor or reeve, or to any justice of the peace having jurisdiction in the Hon. Mr. FISHER.
place,' and not to the officials appointed by the government. The law is apt to be brought into disrepute, if you have an official appointed by the minister called upon not only to give information but to practically try the case he complains about-

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
It may not say that in so many words, but the minister will see that it comes down to that. It provides that if any animal infected with infectious or contagious disease or suspected of being so is sold or exposed for sale ill the market then ' any clerk or inspector, or other officer of the fair or market or any constable or policeman, or any other person authorized by the mayor or reeve, or by any justice of the peace-it is ' place ' in the Bill, but I suppose it means the justice of the ' peace,' and I would suggest that that be corrected-
' or any person authorized or appointed by the minister '-as it is propose'd to be amended-* may seize the animal and report the seizure to the mayor or reeve or to any justice of the peace having jurisdiction in the place '-I suppose that means the municipality-1 and such mayor, reeve, or justice or person authorized or appointed by the minister, may after examination and verification '-cause the animal to be destroyed. Thus, the person appointed by the minister who thinks that an offence has been committed, is practically the informant-properly so, I am not finding fault with that-but it will not help the enforcement of the law if this same officer is to try the case complained of, which his business calls upon him to lay. That will make the law unpopular, and, if it is unpopular it will lose its effect. If the people are not behind a law that law will not be properly enforced. Therefore, I think the minister will help his own case if he would alter the Bill in this respect. Any person arrested or summoned- or it may not be quite that, hut called upon and made liable for a penalty as well as to have his property destroyed-would have his friends in the neighbourhood, who, would, perhaps say he was not guilty of any offence. I would suggest that this section be amended. Let it stand as it is that any clerk or inspector, or other officer of the fair or market or any constable or policeman, or any other person authorized by the mayor, reeve, or by any justice of the peace having jurisdiction in the place-I suppose that means any person specially appointed to enforce this particular law-or any person authorized or appointed by the minister may seize the animal and report the seizure to the mayor or reeve, or to any justice of the peace having jurisdiction in the place. But when it comes to ' and such mayor, reeve, or justice '-that is all right; but I think when it goes on ' or person authorized or appointed by the minister.' may try the case, that would mean that this officer may

enforce his own information. I think the case should be tried by a third person, some one standing between the inspector or the officer, and the person proceeded against, whether he is appointed by the minister or by the head of the municipality, or whether he is one of the ordinary officials of the place. He is one side of the case, he is the complainaut or prosecutor, and I do not think it will make the law more acceptable to the people to put an officer in the position of enforcing his own opinion. He should lay his information before the mayor, reeve or other magistrate, and let that person try the case before the decision is carried out. Then, in the last three lines of this section it provides * to be forthwith destroyed or otherwise disposed of, in such a manner as he deems proper or ns is directed, as provided by this Act.' I do not think that we ought to delegate to the mayor, reeve or other official who is trying the case the power of deciding what we are better able to judge than he. The two hundred and fourteen members of this House are better able to say how this should be done than is the mayor, reeve or other officer. Let him be simply a judicial officer to carry out this Act, but let us say how it is to be carried out.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) does not desire that the officer appointed by the minister should have the power that is given to the reeve, the mayor, or justice of the peace. The mayor, reeve, or justice, as well as the officer appointed by the minister, has the authority to proceed under the first part of the section, and also to judge of the case in tire second part. I do not see any reason why the others should have the power of judging these cases and the inspector appointed by the minister should not have it.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: If the hon. minister will allow me, I do not think he is correct there. I do not understand this to say that the mayor, reeve, justice and so on, may proceed in the first place, but that ' any clerk or inspector, or other officer of the fair or market, or any constable or policeman, or any other person authorized by the mayor or reeve, or by any justice of the peace having jurisdiction in the place,' may proceed. The mayor, reeve, or justice may authorize an officer to proceed, and they may try the cases he brings before them. But the officer appointed by the minister is both complainant and judge.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
I would point out that all through this Bill the matter of prompt and immediate action is the necessity that is recognized, as it was under the old Act. The inspector should be in a position to act promptly, and, so to speak, off-hand. If these officers were not able to seize an animal and deal with it at once, they would not be able to prevent the spread of the disease. The hon. gentleman
will notice that it provides that the officers appointed to deal with these cases ' may after an examination and verification,' cause the animal and so on to be destroyed. The officer may not do this until it is clearly proven to be a case of infectious disease; and when that is proven, it is necessary that he should be able to act at once.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: What do the words ' examination and verification ' mean ? Does it mean a scientific examination of the animal or an examination of witnesses in the ease ? I would like to point out to the minister that a man might be a good judge of beef who would not at all be a judge of whether an animal was diseased or not. I think he should act upon the report of one or two veterinary surgeons, and if that report states that the animal is affected, then lie should give an order for its destruction.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: One of the principles underlying this whole Act is that the veterinaries appointed by the government may have power to act promptly on their own discretion. I think that is absolutely necessary. Of course if these officers were to act improperly and were to give a decision which was not justified by facts, then the government would be responsible. The provision whicli is here discussed is one which has been in existence under the old Act. We are not intensifying it in any way, except that we are asking that the minister may appoint these inspectors instead of the Governor in Council.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Would the minister appoint these justices, or would he allow any other person than justices to act ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The minister only appoints the inspectors, he does not appoint the justices.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I know that, but you give that power to justices of the peace to make this examination. Would you allow any justice to make that examination ? Because it would be a dangerous thing to allow any justice to make such an examination as that, and to act on his own discretion.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The examination contemplated is not made by a justice. This is an examination of a technical character, and has to be made by a veterinary who is properly qualified.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
I think that clause ought to be made a little clearer. It reads now :
And such mayor, reeve or justice, or person authorized or appointed by the Governor in Council may, after examination and verification, cause the animal

And so on. Now that certainly means that a justice of the peace may, after examination and verification, cause the animal affected to be destroyed. It seems to me that a justice of the peace is not the proper per-

son to cause the destruction of that animal, but he is the proper person to inquire and gather the necessary evidence to see whether that animal should be destroyed. It strikes me it would be much better if that clause were framed in this way :
And such mayor, reeve, or justice of the peace, or person authorized or appointed by the Governor in Council, may, after being satisfied by the evidence of a veterinary that such disease exists, cause the destruction of that animal.
Then the justice of the peace would not act on his own judgment, nor would he act on a simple inspection of the animal, but he would act upon the evidence of a man who was thoroughly competent to decide whether the animal was diseased or not. That clause should be amended so as to make it more effective, and to avoid any possibility of error.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I think the word ' verification ' practically covers that point 1 examination and verification.'

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: This Act is to be interpreted by farmers and people who are not perhaps so accustomed to the interpretation of an Act. I think that ought to be made very clear. It seems to me that the language here leaves that matter a little obscure, it may have been so in the old Act. ' Such mayor, reeve or justice, or person authorized may, after examination and verification.' That may mean the justice of the peace, the mayor or the reeve, all those people.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: All the persons authorized.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: So you leave the authority in the hands of the reeve rather than of the government.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: To meet the point raised I would suggest the words ' after the veterinary's examination and verification.' I would be willing to have that inserted.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman any means of knowing whether the veterin-aries are capable men to perform the examination ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: All veterinaries in this country are obliged to have a diploma from a veterinary college before they are allowed to practice, and only those who have such diplomas are entitled to be recognized as veterinaries. In addition to that, the appointees of the department are chosen as veterinaries of standing. knowledge and experience. We make ourselves no examination at the present time to test the qualities of the veterinaries.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows there are some sections where hog cholera may be prevalent, which is a disease Mr. PRINGLE.
of which some veterinaries have very little knowledge. I have in my hand a report of a veterinary whose name, however, I will not mention, in which he says :
Held post mortem examinations on five hogs slaughtered on January 14th, and in examinations could find no indications of bowel trouble, the intestines appearing in each case to be healthy.
That is the report of the veterinary, and in a few days afterwards the whole herd of hogs he mentions were slaughtered. He evidently was not acquainted with hog cholera. I think something should be done whereby veterinaries residing in certain localities where hog cholera is prevalent should be instructed by others who are better posted as to what constitutes hog cholera.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We have tried to do that as much as possible. I think the clause might be simplified by adding these words, ' after verification and examination,'
' or after the magistrate, having been satisfied through evidence that the animal is diseased.' I think that would cover the whole point in a few simple words.

speechtext: I think the suggestion made already will cover that point. The whole essence of this section and of the Bill is to enable prompt action to be taken to prevent the spread of disease. I would not like to see any machinery created which is going to be slow or dragging in its operation.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister what he means by prompt action 1 Whom does he empower to act promptly in the Bill ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The veterinary inspectors have power to do certain things.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: They have power to destroy the animal ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Then, why do you name magistrates, or reeves, or anybody else ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
Because there may be no authorized veterinary inspector present. The magistrate

would then call in a local veterinary of standing, get his opinion and verification as to the disease and order the destruction of the animal effected.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: If a veterinary surgeon was competent to give an opinion would he not be competent to destroy the animal ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes, but we do not give power to any veterinary in the country to do that. We only give that power to inspectors appointed by the Governor in Council and to reeves and magistrates.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Where will the prompt action come in if the veterinary inspector does not happen to be there ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
We cannot always obtain prompt action if there is no veterinary magistrate or reeve in the neighbourhood. I beg to move

I do not think any ordinary person would undertake to deal with that matter, having before him the Act and regulations directing how this should be done.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 11,
The minister may, from time to time, cause to be slaughtered, animals suffering from infectious or contagious disease or suspected of being so affected, and animals which are or have been in contact with or close proximity to a diseased animal, or an animal suspected of being affected by infectious or contagious disease.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Is that not a pretty broad section ?

speechtext:
It is the same as in the former Act except that it substitutes ' minister ' for ' Governor in Council.' In an action of this kind it is
practically impossible to procure an Order in Council when it is necessary.
On section 12,
1.	The Governor in Council may order a compensation to be paid to the owners of animals slaughtered under the provisions of this Act.
2.	Whenever the animal slaughtered was affected by infectious or contagious disease, the compensation shall be one-third of the value of the animal before it became so affected, but shall not in any such case exceed twenty dollars ; in every other case the compensation shall be three-fourths of the value of the animal, but shall not in the case of grade animals exceed fifty dollars, and in the case of pure-bred animals two-thirds of the value of the animal, not to exceed one hundred, and fifty dollars ; and in all such cases the value of the animal shall be determined by the minister or by some person appointed by him.
3.	Such compensation may be withheld in whole or in part whenever the owner or the person having charge of the animal has, in the opinion of the minister been guilty, in relation to the animal, of an offence against this Act, or whenever the animal, being a foreign one, was, in his judgment, diseased at the time of entering Canada.
4.	If in any case the sum received by the government, on the sale of a carcass of an animal slaughtered, under the provisions of this Act. exceeds the amount paid for compensation to the owner of the animal slaughtered, the excess, after deduction of reasonable expenses, shall be paid to the owner.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Would it not be better, so as to make it correspond with the other, to take out the words ' Governor in Council ' and insert the word ' minister ' ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I think, in the matter of compensation which is a question of general policy, that it ought to be decided by the Governor in Council and not upon the minister's own responsibility.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Is this a new section ?
