speechtext:
No.
Mr. POPE, I have known instances ' where animals were slaughtered by authority of some one and they were not diseased at all and no compensation was possible. Can it be a fact that this section has been in operation for a series of years ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will read subsection 3 of this section he will see that it provides that:
Such compensation may be withheld in whole or in part whenever the owner or the person having charge of the animal, has, in the opinion of the minister been guilty, in relation to the animal, of an offence against this Act.
The whole clause is permissive and not compulsory. The question of compensation is a matter entirely within the control of the Governor in Council and is dealt with in regard to each individual case.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I must say that my experience is that the Act might as well not have been printed in so far as the farming community is concerned, because no man is going to complain about the presence of disease in his herds if he is not going to be compensated, and these animals will be disposed of in the future as in the past. There is not a day passing in which there are not diseased animals being disposed of on the market through butchers and by the farmers, and the experience of a man in our community, Mr. Bowen, whom the hon. minister will perhaps know, was not such as to encourage farmers to notify the authorities of the presence of disease because Mr. Bowen's cattle were slaughtered and he got no compensation for them. He lost some animals in which disease could not be traced. He appealed for compensation but did not get it. Under these circumstances no one in the community is going to tell if he has any diseased animals. I found fault with this Act many years ago in regard to this particular. I am sorry that the hon. minister has not seen his way clear to making an amendment to the Act by which compensation would be ensured to those who give information in regard to the presence of disease in their herds. We provide a line of $200 for a person concealing the presence of disease in animals, but we should go further and provide that when a man having the health of the herds of the country and of human beings in view, volunteers this information, he should not find himself in the position in which men giving such information have found themselves in the past. Since this question was discussed several years ago in the House, the increase of tuberculous cattle throughout Canada has been very great. It could have been wiped out by the expenditure of $100,000 or $200,000 at the time, but to-day it would take much more money than that, and the longer it is postponed the greater will be the cost. The day will come when parliament will have to deal with this matter. The object of this Bill is to make a man suspicious of an animal, but if it costs him $50 to be suspicious it will be very hard to impress that suspicion on his mind. I would impress upon the minister that his policy on this matter should be changed. He has the assistance of an ex-member of this House whom we see sitting there to-night, and who is perhaps a better authority on this question than I am, but at the same time I submit that the practical working out of this Act will not tend to improve the health of animals in this country. I do not believe that a man should be compensated who Imports animals and can have them properly inspected before he buys them, but the Canadian farmer who offers his animals for slaughter for the benefit of the community is certainly entitled to compensation. In our section of the country the law has not worked well in the past.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: While I would not like to go as far as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope), I fully appreciate the situation he has depicted. The difficulties are great in securing information about the existence of disease in animals. The idea of compensation to those who report disease among their animals has been discussed upon various occasions in this House. Some years ago, when I asked for a vote to deal with tuberculosis, I had to pledge myself that it would not be used for the purpose of compensation. The hon. gentleman stated that some years ago there was less tuberculosis in Canada than now. I think that statement is-too broad. The tuberculin test has been the means of discovering a great many cases where the existence of the disease would not have been suspected prior to the introduction of the test, but on the whole I am well within the mark when I say that Canada is remarkably free from this disease in comparison with other countries. The question of compensation is a difficult one to deal with. No one would like better than I to give compensation to the public spirited man who offered his animals for slaughter. He ought to be compensated, but the difficulty is to distinguish between such a man and others who would demand compensation, and perhaps obtain it where the necessity for slaughter did not exist. Parliament clearly indicated, when the matter was under discussion before, that it would look favourably at the idea of granting compensation. Suppose we spent a large amount of money and stamped out the disease apparently, yet it is of such a nature that the chances are it would reappear constantly, and although w'e would not have such a large expenditure from year to year as at first, still the expenditure would go on indefinitely. In subsequent sections of the Bill I propose to ask for power to make regulations in regard to certain diseases, and which may help to bring about the state of affairs the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope) refers to.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: If you suspect disease and have animals slaughtered, and if afterwards no disease was found to exist, would the owner be paid in full ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: That would depend on whether the animals would have been In contact with disease or not.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: If they had been in contact, I think you would have the* right to pay the three-fourths of their value, hut if you merely suspect the herd and you order their slaughter, and it was found afterwards that no disease existed. I almost think the owner would be entitled to full compensation.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I would like to have an opportunity of looking into that matter.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I do not suggest tliat the minister should come to any hurried decision on the question. I would advocate killing middling freely when animals are suspected, but if you find you are in error, I think the owner should be fully compensated.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: On one or two occasions we have paid compensation when an error was committed by one of our officers.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: That is what I say you should do.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I think provision should be made for that under the law. I think there is provision in some part of the law, but if not I will see that provision is made.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: With regard to subclause 3, does not the minister think that it would be better to have the matter therein referred to tried in some other way than to leave it to the opinion of the minister ? If a man has been guilty of neglect, it is usually enough to prove it in the locality in which he lives, before some justice of the peace. The minister could not very well determine that down here at Ottawa. He is not going to the place where the man lives, and it will be equally difficult for the man to come to Ottawa.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I do not think the minister could form an opinion on the matter without looking into it very carefully and having the whole evidence before him. Of course, any action of that kind by the minister would be pretty sure to be brought before the House by some one on behalf of the individual if he were discriminated against or hurt. The machinery might be a little awkward in certain cases, but I think it would be safe enough to leave it as it is. It has been in the old Act exactly in this shape.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Although the Governor in Council is to determine the compensation, the minister can withhold the payment of the compensation by deciding that it is not a proper case.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The minister would depend on the report of his own officials who investigated the matter.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Not necessarily. The minister would probably have representations from the individual, and he would have to balance these against the report of his officials. The minister does not depend on his officials in every instance.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
But the person you would call criminal in the matter would be the person attempting to hide the prevalence of disease among his herd. My experience in localities where these things occur is that, without the incentive of compensation, it
is impossible to bring the individual to notify the department of the existence of disease ; the experience is all the other way. The tendency is to hide the fact. There have been cases where the herds have been slaughtered, and after the slaughter it has been found that the disease was not so great as the official has supposed it was. My idea is that it would be better to give a more liberal remuneration, and stamp the disease out as far as possible : it seems to me that is the cheaper way of dealing with the matter. Whether or not the different conditions under which animals are now kept, from the old hardy way, have anything to do with the greater prevalence of disease, I do not know. I think a great many cattle are put into close stables, and too many are put together, which is, no doubt, a cause of disease. You are never going to stamp out the disease unless you let the owner of the cattle understand that it is his interest as well as the community's interest to expose the fact. Take the case of a poor man whose all is represented by the few cows he milks on his farm. That man will hide the fact of disease as long as possible, because if he does not his all will be gone. It would be better for the government to pay him 75 per cent if the animals proved diseased, and 100 per cent if they proved to be not diseased. I do not think you can reach the difficulty in any other way.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I think perhaps the hon. gentleman is labouring under a little misconception. We do not order the slaughter of animals in cases of tuberculosis, which the hon. gentleman evidently has in his mind. At the request of interested individuals, animals supposed to be affected with tuberculosis are inspected, and when found to be diseased, they are subject to the quarantine law, which prevents them being sold or moved about; but no inspector has ever demanded that such animals should be slaughtered.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: But the regulations amount to that. They have to be isolated. The owner cannot take them out of the premises. His only remedy is to kill them. Then he will have an officer of the government along, who will investigate the meat and see that it is not put on the market if it is diseased. It would be better to order the animals to be slaughtered. You would get at the difficulty sooner than you do now.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
The health officers are required to deal with these animals in the interest of the public health. All we try to do is to find out what will benefit the public at large, whether the animal is diseased or not. Then the law steps in and says that if the animal is diseased, it must be treated in such and such a way. That is done in the interest of the public health and for the protec-

tion of the community. I do not think we can relax that law in any way.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: No, but if you take the right to slaughter and remunerate, you will obviate all the other difficulties.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I think the hon. member who has just taken his seat has made a very valuable suggestion. There is no doubt such a tendency as he points out on the part of the people who own cattle which are subject to inspection by a government official, to ascertain whether or not they are diseased if the owner of the cattle were to receive good compensation for the animal slaughtered, he would have no object in concealing the disease or in preventing the official from making a thorough investigation. I think that the suggestion is a very valuable one. If people owning cattle were led to believe that they would be paid in full the value of the slaughtered animals, they would court inspection rather than refuse it, and I believe that would be a very effective way of stamping out the disease. While the government may be very vigilant and have the interests of the farmers at heart, still the farmers do not like to suffer loss, and if they realized that they were going to be fully compensated for the cattle slaughtered, they would court inspection and would be willing to give the government official free access to their herds.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I am afraid that if we were to pay the full value of every animal slaughtered, a farmer who might happen to have surplus stock might be tempted to try and get the value for his surplus animals in this way, and it would be a very dangerous policy to institute. The most that could be expected would be that a certain portion of the value might be paid. If an animal is diseased, the loss is bound to fall on the farmer, and if he be wise he will get rid of the animal. But of course there are some men who will run every risk rather than resort to slaughtering any portion of the herd. It seems to me that to pay the full value would be impracticable. I appreciate what the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) has said, and can realize that so long as we do not pay some compensation, there will be a great deal of difficulty in working out the Act without paying any compensation and the public educated up to the opinion that it is in their own interests not to evade the Act. If we are to inaugurate a system of general slaughter and compensation, I am afraid that we would have to face a very large expenditure, probably from $200,000 to $500,000 per year for several years.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: How can that be when the hon. gentleman told us this session that there was no disease in Canada ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is mistaken. I never said that there was no disease in Canada. There Hon. Mr. FISHER.
is, on the contrary, a considerable amount of tuberculosis in the country. It is a contagious disease which affects animals and men, and I would not venture to say what value would have to be paid if all the animals affected by tuberculosis were to be slaughtered in a few years.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: How could a farmer who has a surplus stock impose upon the government when his herd is inspected by a proper official ? He could not get any of this stock slaughtered without first having the animals inspected by the government veterinary surgeon.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We would have to add largely to the number of our officials, and my experience indicates that we would have to watch with the utmost vigilance. Even now, in the case of hog cholera, when compensation is paid for the hog slaughtered, we have a great deal of difficulty indeed in order to a void being imposed upon, and the difficulty would be much more serious with regard to cattle at large.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can hardly be serious when he makes the charge against the farmers, that when they have surplus stock to dispose of they would take advantage of the law simply for the purpose of making a sale. That is not my estimate of the farmers of Canada. I think that they are a more honourable class of people, and the hon. minister himself, who is a practical farmer, is hardly fair to the farmers of this country when he makes such a wholesale charge.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I hope that my hon. friend will not misquote me. I did not make any wholesale charge, but he must admit that there are among farmers, as in every other section of the country, men who would take advantage of the government if they could.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The hon. minister has not answered the point made by my friend from Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) that the animals slaughtered would not be paid for unless an official of the government had ordered their slaughter. You do not pay for the animal unless you order it to be slaughtered. Then the only ground advanced by the hon. minister for not paying full compensation, is that the farmers are so absolutely unreliable that they would endeavour in the absence of a better market, to work off their surplus stock in this way.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Is the hon. minister aware that there is a good deal of tuberculosis in the country ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
It is well known to exist, not only in this but in other countries.
Mr. R03INSON. But the hon. gentleman said in this country ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Do the British people know this ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: No wonder they keep up the embargo on our cattle.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: There is ten times as much tuberculosis over there as here. It has nothing to do with the embargo. The embargo is on account of pleuro-pneumonia.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will find a report in his department by Dr. McEach-ren, a few years ago, in which he gave the cost of stamping out tuberculosis in this country.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I think he said $200,000 per year for several years.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: For a very few years ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: For several years.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
If it could be accomplished with $200,000 a year for three or four years, it would be money well spent, indeed. I would say again-not that I wish to make a political or a stump speech-that I think the farming community are entitled to an expenditure, even if it reaches a million dollars in a term of years, as much as other portions of the community are entitled to the expenditures we make to assist them in the ways of trade and commerce. In the amount of taxation he bears and in his importance in relation to all other lines of trade, the farmer is the great element of strength in this country, and I believe that the rest of the community would not hesitate to bear their share of any taxation that might be necessary to bring about an improvement so desirable as the stamping out of this contagious disease. As the Minister of Agriculture suggested, this disease is a very stealthy one ; it creeps into a herd of cattle without arousing suspicion, it hangs about the herd for many years without the knowledge of the owner, until a weaker generation of animals come, and then suddenly he finds his whole herd infected with the disease. I would favour compensation for the killing of the animals, for the government has no right to ask that animals be killed, or isolated so that their owners have no use for them, without compensation. A plan should be properly prepared under the direction of medical skill and technical experience, and the House should be asked to vote such money as is necessary in the premises. As this is a government of commissions, it might not be out of place to suggest that we might have a commission with regard to this matter, and then two or three more friends of the government could be given employment for some time. And a
scheme might be formed by which as good results could be obtained as from some other commissions that have been appointed and have caused expenditures certainly not directly beneficial to the farming community. It would also be quite in keeping with matters as we sometimes find them, if a lawyer could be engaged to preside over this commission to look after the interests of the farmers. But joking aside, I think that the importance of the cattle trade in the east and in the west of the Dominion and the importance of the dairy trade, is sufficient to warrant the expenditure, whether it is one hundred thousand, two hundred thousand or three hundred thousand dollars a year, and whether that expenditure is for one year or for the next twenty years.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I shall be happy to consider the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Pope) suggestion of a commission.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I cannot agree with the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) or with the hon. minister that tuberculosis is prevalent in this country.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I think, perhaps, more of the thoroughbred cattle are affected than of the ordinary cattle, but I do not think that there is any justification for such wild charges.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sherritt) is misquoting me. I did not say that tuberculosis is prevalent in this country, on the contrary I said that the herds in Canada were less affected than those of almost any other country. At the same time I said-and it is true-that there is a good deal of tuberculosis among the cattle in Canada.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) that it is desirable to spend even a large sum to stamp out all serious disease affecting our cattle. That is the object of this Bill, but it would appear that the Bill does not go far enough. It is evident from the admission of the minister that there are a great many people who have disease in their herds who do not complain. But the benefit will be small if only a small portion of the diseased cattle are slaughtered, the cattle of farmers who are generous enough to be willing to have them slaughtered and receive only 75 per cent of the value of them if they are not affected, and one-third of the value if they are affected. It is evident to me that if we wish to stamp out the disease, we must take such steps as will ensure the slaughter of ail animals that are affected. And I believe, as has already been said, that, unless the farmer is to get the full value of his cattle, there are many cases in which the farmer will not complain. Why not, then, spend a sufficient sum of money to clear the country absolutely of this disease ? The

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I think that the minister and the House as well, has not allowed for the effect that a clean bill of health for our cattle would have upon the market for our butter and cheese. If it were known that the herds in Canada were clean and free from disease, there Is not the slightest doubt that our products would be more highly appreciated than they can be under any other condition. I think this is something that it is worth while for the country to consider.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
I take strong exception to the Minister of Agriculture telling us that he is afraid that the farmers would impose upon the government of their country by selling their surplus stock under pretense that the cattle were affected with contagious disease. When the minister thinks that over, I believe he will see that he made a statement that he should not have made. As a farmer, I object to a minister of the Crown telling the public that farmers are so mean and low that if they had a few surplus head of cattle they would take advantage of the minister and the government by disposing of them as diseased. Now, why will the minister say that, when he knows deep down in his heart that the cattle cannot be slaughtered without a certificate from the veterinary surgeon ? How could any farmer impose upon the department with diseased cattle in the mean contemptible way he mentions, when he has officials all around the country to inspect the cattle ? I am Mr. SMITH (Wentworth).
here to repudiate any such thing. That may be the prevalent idea with the farmers the Minister of Agriculture associates with, but I can tell him that is not the character of the farmers of Ontario. If it was their disposition, he has it in his power to prevent them dealing with the government in that way. He talks about a few thousand dollars. Who is paying most of the taxation of this country ? Is it not the farming community ? Are not the exports produced by the farming community worth more to this country than any other manufacturing industry in Canada ? And if so, why should a few hundred thousand dollars be parsimoniously dealt out to defend the herds and stock that are bringing more money into this country than any other industry ? You will fritter away two or three hundred thousand dollars in a harbour where there is no harbour, and never will be, and $75,000 to dredge a channel and build a wharf where the post office is not worth $100 a year. That is all right; but when you come to make a clean bill of health for the greatest industry in Canada, you talk about a little expense, and you are afraid the farmers are going to be mean enough to take advantage of the government.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The question of money is not the only one involved here. I presume that hon. gentlemen have followed what is done in other countries in fighting cattle disease, and if so, they must be aware that everything cannot be done by money. If the reputation of our dairy products is high in England, it is not because we have no tuberculosis in this country, but because of the high quality of our product. My hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Smith) has alluded to the experience in some counties in Ontario, to something that was attempted and it failed.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Because they did not pay enough.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Perhaps not; that shows that great difficulty arose in such an undertaking. I think one reason of not paying enough was the opposition of the farmers having their herds compulsorily destroyed. It is not because I am unwilling to pay a sufficient amount, because I think if we could stamp out tuberculosis entirely in this country, a very considerable expenditure would be justified. But we must be able to show parliament that such an expenditure would be successful. My experience leads me to the conclusion that we might go on spending money year after year without really accomplishing the destruction of the disease.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that there is less tuberculosis in this country than in England and the United States ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Then does not the hon. gentleman think it would be well to enter into some different arrangement with the United States, which would prevent their cattle coming in here and feeding in our yards where our own cattle are put afterwards before putting them back on to the farm ? Does not the hon. gentleman think there is something wrong in the present state of affairs when cattle are allowed to be shipped in here from a country where cattle are not as healthy as otir cattle, shipped into our yards, fed in our yards, and our cattle afterwards fed in the same yards ? It seems to me the hon. gentleman has shown a weak point in his argument when he accused the farmers of this country of trying to outwit the officials of the government. It seems to me that the officials of the government ought to be more attentive to their duties, and they should not give certificates at all where there is at least disease.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We do not allow cattle to come in from the United States except for breeding purposes, and they are always tested for tuberculosis. If they are found to be diseased they are not allowed to come in. We do not import Stockers and feeding cattle from the United States except to a certain extent into the North-west Territories.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: What care is taken with regard to cattle coming over from the other side to graze, and then taken back again ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: They are all inspected.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I would like to know if the minister has found the farmers inclined to take advantage of these Acts, and to dispose of animals that are diseased and to get some money return for them ? I do not think, as a rule, he would say that the farmers are apt to take such advantage. There has been a good deal of cattle disease in the county of Pictou, and the hon. gentleman has had something to do with controlling that so-called Pictou cattle disease, and compensating the farmers for animals killed. I do not think he is disposed to argue that generally speaking farmers are dishonest in the matter.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Certainly not. I never undertook to say that.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: That construction has been derived from the language of the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Very improperly.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
I think that a comparatively large amount of money might be expended in stamping out the disease altogether. It will
be cheaper in the end to do that when you take into account the great benefit that will result from a knowledge of the fact that our herds and flocks are entirely free from disease. In the case of the Pictou cattle disease it has been under the care of the government for something like twenty years. I really believe that the government would have saved a great deal of money in connection with this disease, which is still in existence and for which the hon. gentleman is called upon to make payments every year and which has now spread to a distance of nearly sixty or seventy tuples from its original starting point, by adopting the British system used in the case of the Rhinder-pest outbreak and really stamping out the disease by destroying every animal that was either diseased or had come in contact with a diseased animal paying a fair compensation to the farmers for the animals so destroyed. The expenditure already made upon that subject in Nova Scotia I think must be in excess of what it would have cost if every diseased animal, or every animal in contact with diseased animals, had been destroyed and even if the buildings in which they had been housed had been destroyed. I believe the government has paid more than it would have expended if it had destroyed all the animals that have come in contact with diseased animals and replaced the buildings. While you leave the seeds of disease there in animals that are passing back and forward from one farm to another and pasturing together, there is a constant development and growth of the disease it must involve a continual expense. Really, I would imagine it might be in the case of tuberculosis perhaps better to pay the full value if by that means we would be free of the disease, but, I understand, that in reference to tuberculosis the hon. minister would not be prepared to recommend the destruction of the animals effected.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We have never ordered destruction.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
I would rather infer from the experiments conducted on the farm of Senator Edwards that it has been determined that by instructing the farmers sufficiently as to the methods of raising calves from diseased animals these animals continue to possess a certain value in the agricultural sense and that it would be a piece of foolishness to destroy them. But, that being the fact, it seems to me that there should be some system by which farmers would be very carefully instructed as to the means of raising healthy calves from diseased cows and sires, and that certain precautions would be taken to see that milk products from infected animals are not used in such a way as to affect the health of the population of the country. In respect to that I understand that there are experiments making now to determine whether or not the disease is actually communicable from ani-

mals to human beings. I believe there are some parties who do not admit that there is much danger of infection in that way. As long as there is no really demonstrated great danger and as long as there is no question at all as a result of the experiments made under the direction of the hon. minister that diseased animals are quite capable of rearing healthy progeny, I think the hon. gentleman would not be justified in advising the country to go to the heavy expenditure necessary to stamp out tuberculosis. But I think in the case of the so-called Pictou cattle disease, pleuro pneumonia and Rhinderpest, or any other disease that is infectious, the minister would no doubt be warranted in recommending that the animals affected should be slaughtered and that these diseases should be stamped out. I am very glad to hear that the hon. minister has not got an unfavourable opinion of my constituents in connection with the expenditure he has made in so far as the so-called Pictou cattle disease is concerned.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The lion. Minister of Agriculture made a statement to-night that is rather a strange statement for him to make in respect to tuberculosis. I would like to know from the hon. minister if this disease has increased or decreased.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I would not like to say definitely whether it has increased or decreased. My impression is that it is constantly decreasing, because the knowledge of the treatment of the disease is becoming much more widespread amongst the farmers and I know they are dealing with the disease to-day in a way they never thought of doing a few years ago.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
Tuberculosis being a contagious disease, the hon. gentleman has stated that there is a large amount of the disease in Canada, though it is not so prevalent as in the United States or other countries. That being true a statement of that character coming from the hon. minster, I should think would have a tendency to injure our Canadian cattle trade. For the purpose of getting the hon. minister to explain, I will read the statement he made in this House last year in respect to the embargo on Canadian cattle.
I have no hesitation in endorsing that statement-
Referring to the motion made by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa).
The evidence was so completely submitted to the Minister of Agriculture in England, the Hon. Mr. Hanbury, that he first, privately, to myself, when I was interviewing him, acknowledged that there was no disease amongst our animals in Canada against which the provisions of this Act ought to be enforced. When I suggested to him that it would be well to make that statement publicly he shortly afterwards, Mr. BELL.
in an interview, which the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has just been alluding to, made that statement publicly, saying in answer to the assembly of the associations in Edinburgh that he believed to-day that in Canada there was no contagious disease such as they feared the introduction of into England. We therefore say that the evidence has been supplied to Great Britain to show that there is no justification for the application of this Act as against Canadian cattle.
Again be said :
I believe that everybody in Canada who has given the slightest attention to this question of the embargo on our cattle is fully convinced, in the first place, that no disease exists in this country, and, in the second place, that it was not necessary for the protection of the herds in Great Britain. I feel that the parliament and government of Canada can approach the imperial authorities on this question with the greatest force and strength.
Tuberculosis is a contagious disease because tlie interpretation clause says so. We are exporting our cattle to Great Britain. Would it not injure our Canadian cattle trade if it goes abroad that there is a great deal of this contagious disease in Canada, and in view of the statement made by the hon. minister to-night would it not effect the cattle trade in Canada ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: What the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) has quoted is absolutely and entirely correct. The question of the embargo in England is a question as to an embargo on Canada against the introduction of foot and mouth disease and pleuro pneumonia only.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The minister has overlooked the fact that the English Act under which this so-called embargo is levied on our cattle is in general terms. It refers to contagious diseases generally and not to pleuro-pneumonia particularly.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I cannot say positively, but every one knows it was enacted in connection with pleuropneumonia and foot and mouth diseases. There is mange in this country, in the United States and in England, and it is a contagious disease, but the Act does not refer to that.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: There is nothing to prevent the English Act being enlarged at any time if the English government see tit to do so. They claim they have discovered pleuropneumonia in some of our cattle and consequently they simply apply the Act.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: They claimed that years ago, but not now.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: They can embargo our cattle for anything else as well as pleuro-pneu-monia under the Act.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We are allowing United States cattle in bond to be watered and fed in the Toronto stock yards, where our own cattle are brought in after the American cattle leave, and we make no provision for fumigating the stock yards but simply depend in blind faith on the certificate of a gentleman in the United States. It appears to me that there is great danger of disease being introduced in that way. We are making provision in this clause for the destruction of bedding and so on, but we are allowing the condition of affairs in Toronto to go without taking any precaution. It appears to me that it would be a very judicious expenditure to have separate and distinct sheds for American cattle, so that we may not run the risk of the untold damage that may be done if they communicate disease to our animals.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
We do not permit cattle to enter Canada for the purpose of remaining here without submitting them to the tuberculin test, and therefore we ourselves consider the matter a very serious one, so therefore we ourselves consider the matter a very serious one so that we cannot blame the English people for thinking likewise.
I again put myself on record as saying that the expenditure of $200,000 to $300,000 a year if necessary for a term of years, would be a wise expenditure if it resulted in making the health of Canadian cattle better than it is to-day. So far as I am concerned, I am prepared to assume the responsibility of voting for such an expenditure if it were made under proper regulations as no doubt it would be.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
I am quite sure that it is the desire of the minister to do what lie can in the direction of stamping out tuberculosis and all other contagious diseases of cattle. I think from what lias been said on this side of the House that it would be worthy of the minister's consideration as to whether it would not be advisable to offer more compensation to the owners of diseased cattle that have been slaughtered. I
always commend the economical administration of affairs by the government as well as by business men, but at the same time I believe that the only way the minister can succeed is by allowing a fair value for all animals which it is necessary to destroy. I am in hearty accord Avith members on this side of the House who ha\-e spoken on this subject, and they all seem to be of the opinion that it would be money well spent if we made a thorough investigation of the herds throughout the length and breadth of Canada and slaughtered diseased animals lvhere we found them. All owners of cattle Avould assist the minister and his department in trying to eradicate the disease if they got fair compensation for the animals which it was found necessary to destroy. Some members on this side of the House have stated that the agricultural industry is the most important in this country, and I think, Sir, that the agricultural community are entitled to a liberal expenditure for the purpose of stamping out this disease. 1 do not agree with the member for Wellington (Mr. McGowan) avIio stated that tuberculosis was much more prevalent among the higher grade of cattle than among the ordinary herds. I know in my section ef the country where men have pure bred cattle, they have ample provision for stabling them, for ventilating the stables, for taking care of the animals, and they do not allow them to be exposed to severe weather as ordinary herds of cattle are. I believe that today tuberculosis exists to a greater extent among the ordinary herds of cattle in the country than it does among the purer-bred cattle. In conclusion, I advise the minister, Avho I know is very desirous of doing all he can to lessen the prevalence of this disease, to consider the matter fully, and bring down some measure to aid the cattle growers of this country in every way possible to stamp out this disease. I am quite sure they would do all they could in that direction, if they were sure of getting a fair and reasonable compensation.
Section allowed *to stand,
On section 14,-Governor in Council may prohibit importation of animals and certain articles,

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister if there is any Order in Council in existence at the present time prohibiting the importation of animals, or of flesh, hides, hoofs, horns, or other parts of the animal, or of hay, straw, fodder, &c.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes, an Order in Council was passed prohibiting the importation of animals from the neighbouring states in which foot and mouth disease was found to exist, and prohibiting the entry of hides, horns, hoofs, and so on, which were affected.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
Does the minister exercise a supervision over the importation

of hides, not the product of the United States, but coming from a foreign country, say a South American country, through the United States ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
Those hides are allowed in, coming through in bond.
On section 16,

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
This gives the minister power to appoint officers on the spur of the moment, when he thinks it necessary. Under the old Act the Governor in Council had power to appoint, but very often could not appoint until long after the necessity ceased.
On section 17,

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Are the inspectors appointed under this clause and the preceding clause paid an annual salary, or only for their services when called upon ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
That depends on the nature of their engagement. Some inspectors are appointed all the year round on annual salaries ; but this is for the purpose of appointing temporary inspectors for temporary work that arises from time to time, and they are only paid for the work they do.
On section 19-report to Minister of Agriculture.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: This does not seem to provide for the minister having any other information than what the inspector sends. What evidence would the minister have to show him whether the inspector's report was right or not ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The declarations sent in by the inspectors sometimes have to be supplemented by bacteriological investigation ; and if under such circumstances it is found that the disease was not what the inspector thought it was, then the minister would declare that the place was not an affected place. Other cases of that kind might arise.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Is that not a little awkward where you are dealing with portions of the country which are at a very great distance ? For example, suppose you were dealing with a supposedly infected place in a remote portion of British Columbia. It might take a week to communicate with the minister, and the event might show that without any justification it had been regarded as an infected place.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
It would have to be so under the declaration of the local inspector until that was overriden by the report of the inspector-general or the minister. I was pointing out a few minutes ago that sometimes the disease appears to exist, but when the specimens are sent to the laboratory for bacteriological investigation, it is found that Mr. HENDERSON.
the animal is not infected and the minister would reverse the decision of the local inspector.
On section 21,
The area of an infected place may, in all cases of a declaration by the minister, include any common, field, stable, cowshed, or other premises in which infection or contagious disease has been found to exist, and such an area as to the minister seems requisite ; and the minister may, from time to time, by order, extend or curtail the limits of an infected place beyond the boundaries of the common, field, stable, cowshed, farm or premises where infectious or contagious disease is declared or found to exist.
Mr. LANCASTER, Is there to be no chance whatever giveu to the man who is interested on the other side of the question to be heard ? It seems to me that when we give power to enforce an embargo against a man and practically put him out of the cattle-raising business for the season, without giving any or very little compensation, there should be some opportunity given him to present his view of the case.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: It is possible that a veterinary might declare a contagious disease, as for instance, cholera, to be in a certain district for the purpose of getting the fees.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: The inspector is paid a salary and not by fees.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Still it may be in his interest that a district should be declared to be infected. I have an instance in my mind.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: They are not permanent salaried officers ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: That lets in the danger to which my hon. friend referred.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
If we believed that these men were deliberately creating business for themselves, we would have to take steps to remedy that But I do not think that is at all likely, and in any case it is necessary for health purposes that prompt action should be taken. We could not wait for the ordinary procedure of law, and the inspector must take responsibility. If we found him doing anything of the kind without justification, we would soon remove him. At present we are having this work done much more by officers paid by the year and have slightly enlarged our permanent staff, so as to be able to employ permanent instead of temporary officers.
On section 24,

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext:
This provides that an order of the minister relative to an infected

place shall supersede any order of a local authority inconsistent with it. Is not that a little dangerous ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: It has been the rule ever since the Act has been in existence.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I do not think it has ever been tested in the courts. It is a serious thing to put it so strongly as that, without any qualifications, because the question of the power of two parliaments might very easily arise.

Section agreed to.
On section 27,
Every company and every person carrying for hire animals to or in Canada, shall thoroughly cleanse and disinfect, in such manner as the Governor in Council, from time to time, directs, all steamships, steamers, vessels, boats, pens.' carriages, trucks, horse-boxes and vehicles used by such company or person for the carrying of animals ; and the Governor in Council may cause any such steamship, steamer, vessel, boat, carriage, truck, horse-box or vehicle, to be detained at such place as to him seems meet, until it is so cleansed and disinfected.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Has there been any Order in Council passed in connection with this ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman remember the district ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I do not. It is one of the general regulations which require that, any time it is ordered, all railway carriages, trucks and cars for the carrying of stock must be cleansed.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Must cars passing from the United States through Canada into the United States again be cleansed before they return to Canada ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Is the system of keeping track of these cars such that the department knows that they have been thoroughly cleansed ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We have a general order with regard to all cars coming in from the United States. Under ordinary circumstances, there is merely a general inspector to keep track of them. The railway companies are responsible for it, and they are liable to be called to account at any time if they do not comply with the rules. The reports are that they do it very carefully and effectively. When the New England States were scheduled as having foot and mouth disease. we put special officers on and watched so that there should be no danger of cars coming in without being disinfected.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: And how is it with regard to cars coming in from Chicago eastward ? Is the same trouble taken ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: It would not be possible for cars to go from the New England states to Chicago and then into Canada without being cleansed ?	[DOT]

speechtext: The American authorities do not allow the cars to cross into other states from the New England states without being disinfected. They are watching that carefully.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Still, the hon. minister is trusting to their doing it, and is not making any regulation affecting the cars from Chicago ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We have not made any special regulation on that point.

speechtext: In the case of Texas cattle ' going into Alberta. I saw a number of Texas cattle being unloaded there-any one having seen Texas cattie once would have no difficulty in recognizing them again-

speechtext: Are they not Mexican ?

speechtext:
It is south of the Indian Territory, I think.
I think the pan handle of Texas is not included.

speechtext: h>one, by the regulations of the United States. Or, rather, I am informed that I should correct that as to time. There is a certain season of the year when the Texas cattle disease is not dangerous.

When I was acquainted with that section of the country, certain territory was marked out in which the cattie were permitted to be driven from southern Texas through the pan handle and shipped from Dodge city to Kansas city, Chicago and other places. I know that, later in the season^ they are allowed to go anywhere. But during the period of the year when the Texas fever was infectious, the restriction: was imposed. The hon. minister says, as I understand him, that the regulation allow-

ing them to pass through has been done away with.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: That route cannot now be used.

speechtext: The hon. minister thinks there is no danger of the importation of cattle disease into Alberta from that district ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I believe there is none.

speechtext:
Have we regulations prohibiting Texas cattle from coming into Canada ?
The MINISTER OB' AGRICULTURE. We do permit them, with certain certificates from the United States bureau of animal industry, which corresponds to our veterinary bureau-certificates of health aud of individual inspection of the animals- to come into our North-west.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: Could the hon. gentleman say whether these cattle are allowed to come from Texas to other parts of the United States under similar conditions ?

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: I could not tell.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: There is danger in dealing with these cattle, and we cannot be too careful.

subtopic: ACT RESPECTING INFECTIOUS OR CONTAGIOUS DISEASES AFFECTING ANIMALS.
speechtext: We are trying to guard against danger and are watching the matter closely. I think we have been successful in keeping out disease.

speechtext: Will the minister please say which of these sections, from section 17 to section 28 are new ?

speechtext:
Section 26 is new, and section 28 also.
On section 28,
All vards, stables, sheds or other premises used by railway or steamship companies or other persons for the accommodation of animals shall be maintained in a clean, comfortable and sanitary condition, and shall be subject at all times to inspection by inspectors acting under the authority of the minister, who, when they deem such action necessary, may order the cleansing and disinfection in a satisfactory manner of the said yards, stables, sheds or other premises.	, .
2.	In the event of any railway or steamship company or other corporation refusing or neglecting to carry out the orders of_ the inspector in regard to such cleansing or disinfection, or in the event of such company or corporation neglecting to maintain its yards, stables, sheds or other premises for the use of animals, in a clean, comfortable and sanitary condition, the inspector may condemn the said premises ^ as unfit for use ; whereupon the said premises shall not be used for the accommodation of animals until such time as the orders of the inspector in regard thereto have been satisfactorily carried out.

speechtext: I will reserve this section in order to give an opportunity for further discussion. I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Motion agreed to, and progress reported.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE moved the adjournment of the House.

What business shall we expect to-morrow ?
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE We will take up first the Railway Bill, then later on go into Supply.

A week ago I gave notice to the House that I proposed to move a certain motion, and I consented on Thursday last to let the motion stand until to-day. Although I did not make any stipulation about it, I was under the impression that the House would be moved into Committee of Supply to-day, as I extended my motion at tlie request of the government. If the House is to be moved into Committee of Supply to-morrow, it is desirable that the motion should be made at such time as would enable any debate that arose on the motion to be proceeded with and concluded.

In the absence of the Minister of Finance to-night, I would not like to make any pronouncement. But whenever the House does go into Committee of Supply, we will try to meet my hon. friend's views. I do not understand that he desires particularly that that should occur to-morrow; but if the House goes into Committee of Supply tomorrow, we will try to meet the hon, gentleman's wish.

I agreed to permit it' to stand. I said that I would allow it to stand until Monday, which is to-day. Of course, there was no understanding about it other than what would be implied by what took place, which was just about in the words I have endeavoured to give my hon. friend just now.
I will report the matter to the hon. Finance Minister, who will no doubt try to meet the hon. gentleman's views.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.
Tuesday, June 9, 1903.
